items.title: Los Angeles Post-Punk Artist Suffer Well Witnesses the Upheaval of Betrayal in “Came Around”

items.fullText:
You didn’t think that I’d find out,

but I was in the crowd

There is an awful intimacy to betrayal, particularly when the person responsible has mistaken your affection for an inability to see what is happening. You begin to wonder how many ordinary conversations contained a second, concealed conversation, how many reassuring gestures were merely conveniences, and whether the happiness you had begun to trust was ever shared in quite the same way. The discovery can produce an almost embarrassing clarity. Suddenly, every misplaced assurance seems to have been delivered with the confidence of someone who thought the audience had left the room.

On Came Around, Los Angeles musician and filmmaker Alex Delgado, working under the name Suffer Well, explores the uneasy interval between believing that life has finally settled into place and realizing that someone has been quietly dismantling it. Released through God Complex, the hypnotic single draws upon the romantic unease of post-punk, with Joy Division, New Order, and Interpol among Delgado’s acknowledged influences. These artists have each explored the strange compatibility of emotional distress and rhythmic discipline, finding ways to give private anxieties a physical presence.

Delgado, a singer and bassist whose creative work extends into directing and production design, oversees both the music and visual identity of Suffer Well. His multidisciplinary background suggests an interest in how a feeling can be translated into an atmosphere, a character, or a carefully arranged scene. The project occupies that fertile territory where music and cinema share an appreciation for tension, ambiguity, and the expressive possibilities of restraint.

“The song starts with finally feeling like your life is coming together, then someone comes along and upends it,’ Delgado explains.

The crowd is an inspired setting for this particular revelation. It conjures a room full of witnesses, an unsuspecting culprit, and the almost comic arrogance of somebody convinced that discretion and invisibility amount to the same thing. Delgado’s position within that gathering carries a satisfying ambiguity. He may have arrived accidentally, or perhaps suspicion had already led him there. Either possibility lends the lyrics the atmosphere of a scene from a psychological thriller, with the decisive confrontation occurring before anybody has exchanged a word.

Even the title, Came Around, accommodates several interpretations. It might describe the arrival of an unwelcome realization, the return of somebody who has caused considerable damage, or the circular movement of consequences finally catching up with their author. Each possibility carries a different emotional temperature, from resignation to vindication.

Listen to Came Around below:

For Suffer Well, these competing possibilities provide rich material. Delgado finds an uncomfortable kind of comedy in the distance between what people believe they can conceal and what others have already discovered. The song leaves us with a deliciously awkward question: once you realize that somebody has been watching, how confidently can you continue pretending there was nothing to see?

items.title: New Order Announces March 2027 U.S. Tour Dates
items.summary: New Order have announced their first U.S. dates of 2027: a seven-show March run opening at Austin’s Moody Center and closing with two nights at the Fillmore Miami Beach. Future Islands… The post New Order Announces March 2027 U.S. Tour Dates appeared first on
items.fullText:
New Order have announced their first U.S. dates of 2027: a seven-show March run opening at Austin’s Moody Center and closing with two nights at the Fillmore Miami Beach. Future Islands will join the Manchester band for all three Texas dates, while Zachery Allan Starkey is billed for Austin, Fort Worth, New Orleans and Nashville. Longtime collaborator Arthur Baker will DJ both Miami Beach shows; he and New Order co-produced the band’s 1983 single “Confusion.”

The artist presale opens Tuesday, November 10, at 10 a.m. local time with the code Mojito27. General sale begins Friday, November 13, at 10 a.m. local time. Find tickets on New Order’s official tour page.

The announcement comes five days before Joy Division and New Order enter the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame together. The ceremony takes place Saturday, November 14, at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles. The Hall will honor Ian Curtis, Peter Hook, Stephen Morris, Bernard Sumner and Gillian Gilbert. After Curtis’s death in 1980, Hook, Morris and Sumner formed New Order and brought in Gilbert, carrying the urgency of Joy Division into the clubs with records like “Blue Monday.” This was their third nomination, following ballots in 2023 and 2025.

Sumner will also represent Joy Division at the ceremony. Hook, who left New Order in 2007, said in April that he planned to attend and keep his distance from his former bandmates. The day before the induction, he’ll discuss both bands at the GRAMMY Museum in Los Angeles. The recorded ceremony airs on ABC on December 8 from 8 to 11 p.m. ET/PT, then streams on Disney+ and Hulu on December 9.

New Order will play the March dates with touring musicians filling in for drummer Stephen Morris and keyboardist and guitarist Gillian Gilbert. The band said in June that the pair would step away from touring for the foreseeable future. After a September Rolling Stone interview with Morris led to reports that he was seriously ill, Gilbert clarified that he was well and that she was undergoing cancer treatment. “Thankfully, he is well. It is in fact me, who, like many other people, is living with cancer,” Gilbert wrote in a statement asking for privacy during treatment.

Before the U.S. dates, New Order will play six shows across Brazil, Chile, Argentina, Peru and Colombia, starting November 23 in São Paulo and wrapping December 9 in Bogotá. The induction follows a busy year for both catalogs. New Order remastered and expanded (The Best Of) New Order and (The Rest Of) New Order, while Joy Division’s Eternal (Live) box set collects 16 performances, including the Birmingham show where the band played “Ceremony” live for the only time. New Order made it their debut single the following year.

items.title: Aesthetische on ‘Mix The State’, Brazil’s election and the far right
items.summary: Brazilian EBM duo Aesthetische discusses the "Mix The State" EP on Alfa Matrix, Brazil's 2026 election and the rise of the far right.
items.fullText:
Brazilian EBM duo Aesthetische released “Mix The State”, a four-track EP, via Alfa Matrix on November 6, 2026. The Sao Paulo project of Fab Viscardi and Gui Pires built the digital release around its track “Break The State”, first heard on the earlier “Every Beat Matters” EP. In this interview, the duo connects the record to Brazil’s 2026 election, the country’s recent coup trial and what it calls the global rise of the far right.

Aesthetische on Brazil, democracy and the far right

SL: You’ve worked out of Sao Paulo since the Aghast View days. How much does writing a record called “Break The State” from Brazil specifically – rather than Berlin or Brussels – change what the phrase means to you?

Aesthetische: Brazil has become a Country of a large importance to the whole world given that its extension, the importance to Latam and all the natural resources and feedstocks that can be derived from the land. It is also a bio-diversity sanctuary. Obviously it would not get away without being seen as a “geopolitical force to be explored” by oligarch-ran plutocrats like the current US government, fed by the likes of terrible tech-bros and extreme right wing opportunists. Since 2018 with the rise of political movements that culminated with the ascension of Bolsonaro – a fascist at its core (and his family), the Democracy in Brazil has been at stake and if it was not for the power of the people and our institutions we would be today living in a dictatorship again. So, we (the brazilian people) at its majority Broke the State when we reelected Lula (a democratic president in 2022), resisted a coup attempt and arrested the traitors. Every single voice, every one as an individual of resistance (every beat) mattered to deviate the fate of our country to a social-political disaster. This year it happened again, the son of the traitor, a clown who worked for money to the interests of the American Government tried to get elected using his father inherited political views – and he almost did it. Fortunately the majority of the Brazilian people exploded into a democratic movement that sent millions of unlikely voters (like sick and disabled, old people and the minorities) to the voting polls and we kept the Democracy in place with a Center-Left president in place.

SL: This EP lands at the close of a bruising election year at home: a first round the right led, an October runoff that returned Lula for a fourth term, and a losing candidate who rejected the count. Did any of that bleed into the writing, or was the record finished before the campaign peaked?

Aesthetische: It was recorded before but we were aware we needed to be part of the democratic movement that took the Country by Storm, each and every individual had a very important role to move the wave towards the second round of the elections, ensuring the reelection of a democratic president.

SL: The last few years in Brazil have put the machinery of the state on full display – a former president convicted over a coup plot, courts expanding their reach, thousands of police killings, facial recognition turned on protesters. When you sing “break the state,” which state are you picturing?

Aesthetische: We are picturing the authoritarianism plutocrat right led politicians who work as new colonies to the far right power in place today in America.

SL: Some Brazilians look at that same stretch and see institutions holding the line against an attempted coup; others see a judiciary that has grown too powerful. A slogan flattens that into one raised fist. Does the nuance matter to you, or is the slogan doing a different job?

Aesthetische: Facts cannot be changed, what we do with them nevertheless, defines our future as a country and as a free and prosperous people. If you see what not holding the US president accountable for their (USA) attempted coup and the results to their country and to the geopolitical situation of the World and compare it with what Brazil did, you will get the answer I guess. You can also see what alignment to the right wing plutocrats did to Argentina. Their country is under 40% of poverty – levels never seen before, rights have been depleted from the population and the rich (even their president) getting richer by exploiting this terrible scenario.

SL: Washington weighed in this cycle – tariffs on Brazil, sanctions on judges, a US president openly backing one side. How does it feel to make anti-authority music while your country’s politics are pulled at from outside?

Aesthetische: We are trying to play our part not only as musicians but being part of a World being threatened by the rise of the Far-right.

SL: Industrial and EBM have always played with the imagery of power – uniforms, commands, martial rhythm – while claiming to oppose it. Working from a country with living memory of dictatorship, how do you stay on the right side of that line?

Aesthetische: We try to stay on the right side not letting our memories get erased (Brazil was a dictatorship before the 80s) and we had a negationist right wing fascist in power again from 2019 to 2022), defending diversity of people, of genders, of religion and raising a flag to those who are mostly in need, to those who need people to defend their rights, those that need representation because their voices are trying to be shut by selfish plutocrats who detain the economic power and are backed by a corrupt and manipulated hoard of tech bros.

The state now: apps, platforms and power

SL: For a lot of people the state they deal with daily isn’t a parliament – it’s an app, a payment rail, a face scanner, an algorithm deciding a benefit. Is that the real “alarm state” now?

Aesthetische: Yes, all of that can be used as weapons of manipulation trying to attract and mislead the masses into the fascist realm.

SL: Power has drained toward things that aren’t governments at all – platforms, payment networks, a handful of tech owners. When you aim at “the state,” are you aiming at the wrong target, or has the target simply changed shape?

Aesthetische: If you listen to our EP – “Selling Fear” – from last year – we were targeting exactly that. Fascism uses the power of the tools they have at hand to spread fear and misinformation at governmental level if that is not fought by those who know history. It is not this or that – not tech owners or the state (governments and political power) – it is exactly the alliance that can be formed by this coalition when all what matters is defending the supremacy of an economical elite – mostly driven by white male pseudo christian plutocrats. Our ep Every Beat Matters and Mix the State are a follow-up to Selling Fear.

SL: Borders, passports and deportation are hardening worldwide at the same moment capital and data cross them freely. Does the nation-state feel stronger or weaker to you than when you started making music?

Aesthetische: It is certainly different. Money and Power has always been able to get the pace of things at their favor and it has certainly contaminated the world into something we expected not to see anymore. The rise of the right, Wars taking place, coup-attempts, prejudice, white supremacism and intolerance.

A state worth defending

SL: Is there a version of “the state” you’d defend?

Aesthetische: Yes, a state that works FOR or on BEHALF of its people, its sovereignty, its culture, its social welfare, which is inclusive, free and that operates to protect our environment and to collaborate with other countries and economies on behalf of humanity. Call us utopic, but that is our vision.

SL: If a listener in Brasilia and a listener in Brussels take opposite politics from the same track, is that a failure of the song or exactly what you wanted?

Aesthetische: Well, if the listener know who we are and what we stand for it is unlikely to be on the wrong side. Political pluralism is great and wanted. What we do not tolerate is the rise of totalitarian plutocratic belic power and the oppression imposed to humanity from their representatives. Democracy should always win.

About Aesthetische

Aesthetische is a Brazilian EBM and electro-industrial duo based in Sao Paulo, formed by Fab Viscardi and Gui Pires, who had previously worked together in the Brazilian act Aghast View and in Biopsy. The duo debuted on the Belgian label Alfa Matrix in 2012 with the album “Powerswitch” and has issued a steady run of albums, EPs and singles through the label since, including “HybridCore” (2014) and “Rvprty” (2022). More recent EPs include “Boiling Over” (2023), “Confidence Is Silent” (2024), the six-track EPCD “Selling Fear” (2025) and “Every Beat Matters” (2026).

“Mix The State” extends the anti-extremism theme the duo set out on “Every Beat Matters”, reworking “Break The State” into a harsher “static noise version” and a club-focused “electric hell version” alongside the previously unreleased “Alarmstate”.

items.title: Carrellee shares video for new single ‘Waiting’, confirms European tour with Bragolin
items.summary: Madison darkwave artist Carrellee releases single "Waiting" with a self-directed video, and opens for Bragolin on a 21-date European tour from November 12.
items.fullText:
Madison, Wisconsin darkwave artist Carrellee has released a new single, “Waiting”, on November 6, 2026, with a self-directed video, ahead of a 21-date European tour opening for Dutch act Bragolin.

Carrellee wrote, performed and produced “Waiting” herself, pulling the track toward the techno and dance-pop sounds of the late 1990s and early 2000s. Maurizio Baggio, known for his work with The Soft Moon and Boy Harsher, mixed the track, and Josh Bonati, who has mastered for Adrianne Lenker, handled mastering; both also worked on Carrellee’s self-titled 2025 album for Young & Cold Records. The cover art is by miggymagic. Carrellee directed and shot the video herself, in a mix of outdoor and home settings.

“Waiting” is available now on Bandcamp and streaming platforms.

Carrellee and Bragolin European tour dates

Carrellee opens for Bragolin on a 21-date European tour running from November 12 to December 19, 2026:

About Carrellee

Carrellee is a darkwave artist based in Madison, Wisconsin, who writes, performs and produces her own material. She debuted in 2022 with the album “Scale of Dreams” on Negative Gain Productions, later reissued by No Coast Records, followed in 2023 by the remix album “Rescaled” and a video for “Stay”.

In 2025, Carrellee released her self-titled second album on Young & Cold Records, mixed by Maurizio Baggio and mastered by Josh Bonati, with “Captain” as its breakout single. Between 2023 and 2025 she worked with IAMX, including an IAMX remix of her single “Like a Ghost”, and in 2026 she completed a 30-date US tour.

Carrellee’s new single, “Waiting”, continues the same production partnership behind her 2025 album, and precedes a 21-date European tour opening for Bragolin that begins November 12, 2026.

items.title: Anton shares video for new single ‘Serpent Des Villes’, first taste of EP ‘Tôt Ou Tard’
items.summary: Paris post-punk project Anton releases single "Serpent Des Villes" with a video, the first taste of the upcoming EP "Tôt Ou Tard" on Icy Cold Records.
items.fullText:
Paris-based post-punk project Anton has released a new single, “Serpent Des Villes”, with an accompanying video, on November 6, 2026. The track is the first single from Anton’s forthcoming EP, “Tôt Ou Tard”, on Icy Cold Records.

Anton Steinbock mixed and mastered “Serpent Des Villes” himself. Sung in French, the track pairs an organ-like synth and drum machine with wiry post-punk guitar. Its video shows Steinbock alone in a Paris park.

“Serpent Des Villes” is available now on Bandcamp and streaming platforms, including Spotify and Apple Music.

Anton’s ‘Serpent Des Villes’ follows ‘Glacier / Volcan’

Steinbock launched Anton as a solo darkwave project in Paris in 2024, releasing the debut EP “Volcan” that May. Icy Cold Records followed with “Glacier / Volcan”, covered by Side-Line in 2025, pairing that EP with new material including the track “L’Autre Destination”. Anton released the double single “Never Freed Myself” in February 2026, and “Serpent Des Villes” is the first single from the EP “Tôt Ou Tard”, also on Icy Cold Records.

About Anton

Anton is a solo darkwave project led by Paris-based musician Anton Steinbock since 2024, drawing on bands such as Joy Division and Lebanon Hanover while singing across French, German and English. The project’s debut EP, “Volcan”, arrived in May 2024, followed in March 2025 by “Glacier / Volcan” on Icy Cold Records, which combined the debut with newer material including “L’Autre Destination”. Anton played its first international shows in Italy at the end of 2025.

In February 2026, Anton released the double single “Never Freed Myself”. Side-Line covered “Glacier / Volcan” on its release. Anton’s new single, “Serpent Des Villes”, released November 6, 2026, is the first taste of the forthcoming EP “Tôt Ou Tard”, again on Icy Cold Records.

items.title: Bella Eterna releases second album ‘2Faces’, shares video for ‘When I Grow Up’
items.summary: Belgian-Spanish darkwave duo Bella Eterna releases second album "2Faces" via Mots Music, with a video for opening track "When I Grow Up".
items.fullText:
Belgian-Spanish darkwave duo Bella Eterna has released its second album, “2Faces”, via Berlin label Mots Music, alongside a video for the opening track “When I Grow Up”.

The Mots Music edition of “2Faces” lists a release date of October 30, 2026; Bella Eterna’s own Bandcamp page lists November 6, 2026. The album is out digitally and as a limited 12″ vinyl pressed in an edition of 100 black copies, with the digital edition also sold through the band’s own Bandcamp page.

“2Faces” runs nine tracks: “When I Grow Up”, “Break the Cage”, “2Faces”, “Magic Tree”, “Pink Teddy”, “Ballet For Sea Gods”, “Burn”, “When I Grow Up” (Cycle Remix by David Kano and Juanjo Reig), and “2Faces” (Parissior Remix). JG Outsider wrote, programmed and mixed the album; Gerd Van Geel wrote the lyrics and sings. It was mastered at Monoposto Mastering, with cover photography by Domingo J. Casas. The “When I Grow Up” video, set in a circus, has no credited director.

Bella Eterna pairs Van Geel, former drummer and later singer of Belgian band The Arch, with Spanish producer and DJ JG Outsider (Javier Gómez), who is based in Murcia. The project grew out of two reworkings of The Arch material: a 2020 remix of “Phantom Chase” and a 2023 revisit of “Ribdancer” for a Banshees Records tribute compilation.

Bella Eterna’s ‘2Faces’ follows 2024 debut ‘Pornographic Shadows’

Bella Eterna released its debut album, “Pornographic Shadows”, through Unknown Pleasures Records in 2024, followed by the “Fire” EP on Strict Tempo in 2025, which included an Alpha Sect remix of “Me and the Desert”. “2Faces” is the duo’s second full album and its first release through Mots Music.

About Bella Eterna

Bella Eterna was formed in Belgium by Gerd Van Geel, formerly the drummer and later lead singer of Belgian band The Arch, founded in Breendonk in 1986. Van Geel became Bella Eterna’s vocalist after producer Ludo Camberlin had band members try out The Arch’s vocal parts, and he also directed the Bella Eterna video “Mysterious Beauty”, taken from the “Fire” EP.

The project’s Spanish half, JG Outsider (Javier Gómez), is a producer and DJ born in Alicante and based in Murcia, active since 1984. He has produced for the Pink Records label since 1992, and released the 2024 track “Despierto” for Cold Transmission under the JG Outsider name.

Bella Eterna grew out of two reworkings of songs by The Arch: a 2020 remix of “Phantom Chase” and a 2023 revisit of “Ribdancer”, a track the band’s Bandcamp describes as a cult favourite in Spain, made for a Banshees Records tribute compilation. The duo released its debut album, “Pornographic Shadows”, through Unknown Pleasures Records in 2024, followed in 2025 by the “Fire” EP on Strict Tempo, which included an Alpha Sect remix of the track “Me and the Desert”.

Bella Eterna’s second album, “2Faces”, arrives via Mots Music, pairing a digital release with a limited 100-copy black vinyl edition, and is introduced by a video for its opening track, “When I Grow Up”.

items.title: Billy Zach releases third album ‘A Little Hope’ on La Pochette Surprise
items.summary: Hamburg post-punk band Billy Zach released its third album "A Little Hope" on October 30, 2026 via La Pochette Surprise Records, now on Bandcamp.
items.fullText:
Hamburg-based post-punk band Billy Zach released its third studio album, “A Little Hope”, on October 30, 2026, via La Pochette Surprise Records.

The nine-track album was recorded live by the quartet and follows the band’s 2024 EP “Interferer”. A press summary describes the record’s tone: “Anyone who thinks Billy Zach wants to offer hope with ‘a little hope’ is mistaken. Rather, it’s about that last glimmer of hope just before giving up.” The songs include “Therapy”, about failed attempts at therapy, “German Angst”, about collective anxiety, and “Ideals”, about false ideals, alongside more driving, hook-based tracks such as “Pointed Shoes”, “1.8 Million” and “Out of Time”.

Bandcamp’s own description of the release notes that the band “vent collective anxieties on their gnarled, live-recorded new album, deploying catchy hooks on a nonstop basis.” A video for the single “Cede” and a live session of “German Angst” are available on the band’s YouTube channel. “A Little Hope” is also available as a limited-edition 12″ orange-splatter vinyl LP through La Pochette Surprise Records.

About Billy Zach

Billy Zach is a post-punk quartet from Hamburg, Germany, drawing comparisons to acts such as Fontaines D.C., Interpol and Nick Cave. The band’s back catalogue includes the albums “A Momentary Bliss” and “I Am You”, along with the 2024 EP “Interferer”. “A Little Hope”, released October 30, 2026 via La Pochette Surprise Records, is the band’s third studio album.

items.title: Arsine Tibé to release ‘The Lounge Noire Sessions (Episode IV)’ on 13 November
items.summary: German project Arsine Tibé releases the instrumental EP "The Lounge Noire Sessions (Episode IV)" as a self-release on November 13, 2026.
items.fullText:
On November 13, 2026, Arsine Tibé self-releases the instrumental EP “The Lounge Noire Sessions (Episode IV)”, the fourth instalment of a series that began earlier in 2026. The three-track EP runs “SynthPunk”, “Computer” and “Der Traum von einem sorgenlosen Leben”, all composed, arranged, produced and mixed by Manfred Thomaser.

Where the first three Lounge Noire Sessions EPs mixed trance, disco, Motown and jazz influences, Episode IV moves toward 1980s synth-pop and new wave reference points. Reviewer Torsten Pape, writing in the EP’s own press materials, described the opening two tracks: “Particularly on the first two tracks, ‘SynthPunk’ and ‘Computer’, Kraftwerk meets Duran Duran, or even Level 42 and ABC (though still in a purely instrumental version).” Of the closing track, “Der Traum von einem sorgenlosen Leben”, Pape wrote: “[it] has what it takes to serve as the theme tune to a sitcom from that era,” drawing a line to “The Second Coming Of Time” from Episode II. No streaming or purchase links for the EP have gone live yet ahead of the November 13 release date.

About Arsine Tibé

Arsine Tibé is the Lounge Noire and electronic pop solo project of Manfred Thomaser, based in Munich, Germany. He is best known as one half of !Distain, the German synthpop duo he shares with Alexander Braun, and has also worked on the projects Demokratie and The Independent Seasons.

Side-Line first covered Arsine Tibé in February 2016, when Thomaser launched a mini-album under the project name. In 2026 he opened the Lounge Noire Sessions series with Episode I, followed by “The Lounge Noire Sessions (Episode II)” on June 19 and “The Lounge Noire Sessions (Episode III)” on October 2. Between those two, Arsine Tibé and vocalist Suzanne Letting released the concept mini-album “Reclaimed” on August 7, 2026. “The Lounge Noire Sessions (Episode IV)”, out November 13, continues the instrumental EP series.

items.title: Black Lung opens pre-order for ‘Ordo Ab Chao’ LP on Ant-Zen
items.summary: Black Lung opens pre-order for the live album "Ordo Ab Chao", recorded at Paris' Temple des 33 Masonic lodge, out November 16 on Ant-Zen as a marbled vinyl LP.
items.fullText:
Australian artist David Thrussell, recording as Black Lung, has opened pre-orders for the LP “Ordo Ab Chao”, set for release November 16, 2026 on the German label Ant-Zen.

The album was recorded live at a private concert in the Temple des 33, a Masonic lodge in Paris, France, on June 21, 2026. Guest performers on the recording include Atom™, Byron Scullin (Spiderface), thereminist Miles Brown and synthesist Darrin Verhagen of Shinjuku Thief. All tracks were written by Thrussell, except “De Profundis” (Thrussell/Scullin/Brown) and “Order Out Of Chaos” (Thrussell/Verhagen). The album was mastered by Alvin Lucia at the Iron Mountain Analogue Research Facility, with artwork by Richard Grant and layout by Salt; vinyl cutting is by Stefan Betke (Pole) at Scape Mastering.

The LP is pressed on limited-edition 12″ multi-coloured turquoise-blue marbled vinyl, with each copy pressed in a unique colour blend, packaged in a full-colour inside-out print sleeve with a digital download code.

About Black Lung

Black Lung is the solo project of Australian artist David Thrussell, also known for his work with Snog and Soma. Thrussell’s catalogue under the Black Lung name has centred on Ant-Zen releases, including the 2026 ritual LP “The Reign Of Dead Matter”. In September 2026 he announced European shows alongside Snog, and in October 2026 discussed his work in a wide-ranging Side-Line interview.

“Ordo Ab Chao”, out November 16, 2026 on Ant-Zen, documents a private live performance at the Temple des 33 in Paris and features contributions from Atom™, Byron Scullin, Miles Brown and Darrin Verhagen.

items.title: Damage Control and Left Spine Down release collaborative EP ‘Blackout’
items.summary: Damage Control and Left Spine Down release the collaborative EP "Blackout" via Metropolis Records, three tracks produced and mixed by Chris Peterson.
items.fullText:
Australian electro-industrial group Damage Control released the collaborative EP “Blackout” with Canadian act Left Spine Down on November 6, 2026, via Metropolis Records.

“Blackout” consists of three songs written and recorded by Damage Control in collaboration with Left Spine Down (LSD), co-founded by Kaine Delay (vocals, guitar) and Matt Girvan (guitar) in Vancouver in 2001, whose most recent line-up also included Galen Waling (drums). The tracklist runs “Saboteur”, “Unperson” and “Blackout”, produced and mixed by Chris Peterson and mastered by Greg Reely.

Damage Control’s Bill Barsby commented on the collaboration: “I had always enjoyed the music of LSD and I think we managed to smash out a great collaboration with Kaine here. ‘Saboteur’ and ‘Blackout’ are the kind of tracks to get played at a club, but I also love the moodier ‘Unperson’.”

Kaine Delay described the EP’s lyrical tone: “If you’re listening to the EP and you feel seen in that ugly, uncomfortable way – good. That’s the point. I wasn’t trying to write anthems. I was trying to write a transmission from inside the blackout, for anyone else still awake in it.”

“Blackout” follows two other 2026 collaborative EPs from Damage Control: “Master Of Silence”, four songs recorded with Danish musician Claus Larsen of Leæther Strip, and “Red Lines”, three songs recorded with Canadian duo OHMelectronic.

About Damage Control

Damage Control is an international electro-industrial group centred around a core trio of Bill Barsby, Richard Thacker and Alex Wise, all based in Australia, with Barsby and Thacker originally from the UK. The group built its catalogue around a series of collaborative releases, including the January 2026 single “Rage” with Leæther Strip’s Claus Larsen, which led into the four-track EP “Master Of Silence” with the same collaborator.

Later in 2026 Damage Control released “Red Lines”, a three-song EP recorded with the Canadian duo OHMelectronic. “Blackout”, released November 6, 2026 via Metropolis Records, continues that run of collaborations, pairing the group with Left Spine Down’s Kaine Delay for three tracks mixed by Chris Peterson and mastered by Greg Reely.

Left Spine Down was co-founded by Kaine Delay (vocals, guitar) and Matt Girvan (guitar) in Vancouver in 2001; its most recent line-up also included drummer Galen Waling.

Swedish electronica and darkwave duo BAST released a collaborative single with synth collective KÅRP, “S K L L”, on October 30, 2026, through Red Round Records.

BAST consists of John Lönnmyr, also a member of The Night Flight Orchestra, and Daniel J, who has performed as a solo artist and worked professionally in the music industry for many years. The duo released its debut EP, “Together In Violence”, on Red Round Records in 2025, a 12″ vinyl release combining synth-pop and darkwave. BAST has played sold-out shows and festival gigs, and is booked to appear at Sweden’s Subkultfestivalen in 2027.

KÅRP works within its own genre description, death-disco. Anna-Maria Lundberg, described as the project’s vocal presence, commented on the collaboration: “It’s an honor to have been able to tinker with little melodies and be a small part of BAST’s beautiful S K L L.”

“S K L L” was recorded by BAST and KÅRP and mixed by BAST. Hans Olsson handled mastering at Svenska Grammofonstudion. The single is available now on Spotify and other digital platforms.

About BAST

BAST is a Swedish electronica and darkwave duo formed by John Lönnmyr and Daniel J. Lönnmyr is also a member of The Night Flight Orchestra, while Daniel J has worked as a solo artist and in the music industry professionally for many years.

The duo released its debut EP, “Together In Violence”, in 2025 on Red Round Records, issued as a limited 12″ vinyl EP combining synth-pop and darkwave influences. BAST has played sold-out club shows and festival dates, with a 2027 appearance confirmed at Subkultfestivalen, Sweden’s largest festival for alternative music.

“S K L L”, released October 30, 2026 via Red Round Records, is BAST’s latest single and its first released collaboration with synth collective KÅRP.

items.title: Sorrow Makes a Stranger of the Self in Berlin Post-Punk Artist Rosa Damask’s Video for “Crygirl”
items.summary: I can’t understand What’s going on in my mind Sorrow can make you miss yourself. You remember how easily you once spoke to people, the plans that gave your days… The post Sorrow Makes a Stranger of the Self in Berlin Post-Punk Artist Rosa Damask’s Video for “C
items.fullText:
I can’t understand
What’s going on in my mind

Sorrow can make you miss yourself. You remember how easily you once spoke to people, the plans that gave your days direction, the feeling of being present in your own life. Losing that familiarity leaves you trying to explain a change you can barely understand, while the people who know you best seem to be speaking to someone you remember being. The distance becomes harder to bear when you start blaming yourself for it.

That estrangement runs through Crygirl, the latest single from Berlin artist Rosa Damask. Nastia Reigel, the musician behind the project, sings of a mind she struggles to understand, the effort to belong, and the sense that her old dreams have gone on without her. The refrain keeps returning to how different she feels, worrying at a realization she cannot quite account for.

The title might be an admonition muttered at her own reflection. Crygirl has the sting of a name that makes a complicated sadness sound childish, something she ought to have learned to bear more elegantly. Heard that way, it adds a second wound to the song, the shame of needing comfort when she has already begun to lose patience with herself.

Reigel’s smoky, intimate vocal carries a PJ Harvey sultriness, the words unfolding slowly over a bass line that hums and throbs. Drums land with a heavy thump, cymbals splash through the spaces around her voice, and a thick guitar riff with the romantic weight of The Cure leads into the chorus. Sighing synth pads deepen the ache, giving the refrain a weary tenderness. Her voice stays close through the swell, inviting the listener into a vulnerable moment while she is still finding the words for it.

Andrii Kaplia’s video for the song surrounds Reigel with burgundy carpets, patterned wallpaper, and gilt mirrors. In a black suit with pale ties trailing from her cuffs, Reigel crawls across the floor, folds into corners, and raises her hands beside her reflection. Her restless movements disturb the rooms’ faded formality. The mirrors keep placing another version of her in the frame, turning each private gesture into an encounter with herself.

Watch the video for Crygirl below:

Listen to Crygirl below and order the single here

Rosa Damask is the solo project of Nastia Reigel, a Berlin-based musician and producer who came up in St. Petersburg’s techno scene. She founded the queer club night Грань (Grahn’) there in 2018 and has composed music for art-house films. Rosa Damask appeared on Vatican Shadow’s Berghain Mix 09 before releasing music through his Hospital Productions label. Recordings Reigel made between 2018 and 2020 became the basis for her diary-like 2021 release on DKA, Memorials.

On Adore You, her album for Downwards Records, Reigel brought the economy of her electronic work to guitar-led post-punk. The album’s “Bored” appeared in Versace’s Fall/Winter 2025 runway show in Milan. Kaplia directed the title-track video and filmed Reigel’s live performances at Morphine Raum and Silent Space.

items.title: David J releases new single ‘Walking With The Angels’
items.summary: Bauhaus and Love and Rockets co-founder David J releases single "Walking With The Angels" ahead of new album "Postcards From The Afterlife", out Nov 27.
items.fullText:
Alternative rock musician David J released a new single, “Walking With The Angels”, on November 6, 2026, through Label 51 Recordings. J is the co-founder of post-punk bands Bauhaus and Love and Rockets.

“Walking With The Angels” was recorded in Prague using musicians from the city’s Symphony and Philharmonic Orchestras, selected by lead violinist Karel Holas, with Jan Valta orchestrating and conducting. “The song came about very spontaneously, as I was actually there to produce an incredibly talented singer-songwriter who shall remain nameless,” J said. “However, he had some very self-destructive traits and was in no fit state to enter the studio, so the sessions were cancelled. But, we still had the orchestra booked for two days, so I stayed up all night writing this song about the situation, venting my frustration over what had gone on. I went into the studio the next day and did the vocal in one take.”

The accompanying video was directed by actor Marc Warren, known for the series “Van der Valk”, who attended the Prague recording session. “I had the good fortune to witness the inspiration, birth and production of the song, which had a synchronicity to it that only the magic of Prague could manifest,” Warren said of the shoot, which was filmed as a single take of J performing in front of a projected, out-of-focus visual reference for the song.

“Walking With The Angels” follows the previously released “Requiem For The Rose Garden”, and both tracks appear on David J’s new album, “Postcards From The Afterlife”, out November 27, 2026 via Label 51 Recordings on 2xLP coloured vinyl, CD and digital formats. The fourteen-track album features a cast of musicians including multi-instrumentalist Julian Shah-Tayler, who co-wrote three tracks with J.

J said of the record: “This album is essentially about the poignant persistence of connection, be it in life or in death. Schisms and transitions. Love found and love lost. Requiems, reflection and revelation.” The cover is a painting by artist Stefan Prince featuring an owl. J describes the album as one that “acts as an escort of sorts, leading the listener through the corridors of the liminal where some doors close as others open and the moon illuminates the path.”

David J tour dates

David J tours the UK and Europe through November and December 2026, with Paul Wallfisch (ex Swans) as a special guest on every date and Fiona Brice joining for the UK shows:

  • November 27: Porto, Portugal, Auditório CCOP
  • November 28: Lisbon, Portugal, RCA Club
  • December 1: London, UK, Moth Club
  • December 2: Reading, UK, Face Bar
  • December 4: Hebden Bridge, UK, Trades Club
  • December 5: Liverpool, UK, Rough Trade
  • December 8: Edinburgh, UK, The Voodoo Rooms
  • December 9: Glasgow, UK, Stereo
  • December 10: Newcastle, UK, The Cluny
  • December 11: Birmingham, UK, Hare & Hounds
  • December 13: Brighton, UK, Daltons
  • December 15: Athens, Greece, Death Disco
  • December 17: Berlin, Germany, Frannz Club

About David J

David J, born David John Haskins, is an English alternative rock musician, producer, writer and artist from Northampton, England, now based in Los Angeles. He co-founded the post-punk band Bauhaus in 1978, playing bass and co-writing the group’s songs. After Bauhaus split in 1983, he formed Love and Rockets with two of his former bandmates. He was the group’s bassist, co-vocalist and co-songwriter across seven albums released between 1985 and 1998. Both bands have reformed periodically since.

Before Bauhaus split, J had already begun a solo career, and spent two years as bassist and co-producer for The Jazz Butcher, the alias of the late Pat Fish, prior to forming Love and Rockets. He has released sixteen solo albums to date, alongside work across film and theatre, and collaborations with other artists. His memoir, “Who Killed Mister Moonlight?”, was published in 2014.

David J’s seventeenth solo album, “Postcards From The Afterlife”, follows the single “Requiem For The Rose Garden” and is out November 27, 2026 via Label 51 Recordings, alongside a run of UK and European tour dates in November and December.

items.title: Night Nail releases fourth album ‘Infinite Fountain’ via Icy Cold Records
items.summary: Berlin darkwave artist Night Nail releases fourth album "Infinite Fountain" via Icy Cold Records, mixed by William Faith of Faith and the Muse.
items.fullText:
Berlin, Germany-based darkwave artist Night Nail has released its fourth studio album, “Infinite Fountain”, out now via Icy Cold Records of France.

The album’s title reflects its cyclical structure: the opening notes of the track “Vile Train” return, reprocessed through synths, on the closing track “Gloom And Doom”, closing the record where it began. Night Nail’s Brandon says of the title: “I envision a fountain of water or love, eternally giving beauty to the world. As long as I make music, I am that fountain.”

“Infinite Fountain” was mixed and post-produced by William Faith, known for his work with Faith and the Muse, Christian Death, Mephisto Walz, Shadow Project and The March Violets, at 13 Studio in Chicago, Illinois. The album was also mixed and produced by Sven Wolff at Cosmonaut Studio in Berlin. Additional vocals and guitar were supplied by VV & the Void, with additional bass guitar by Kill Shelter.

The album follows two advance singles, “Vile Train” and “Passion Squad”, both released by Side-Line earlier in 2026 ahead of the full-length.

“Infinite Fountain” is out now on a limited edition CD through Icy Cold Records, and on Bandcamp, Spotify and other digital and streaming platforms.

About Night Nail

Night Nail is a darkwave project based in Berlin, Germany, fronted by Brandon. Side-Line first covered the “Infinite Fountain” album campaign in September 2026, when Night Nail shared the single “Vile Train”, followed by a second single, “Passion Squad”, in October 2026.

“Infinite Fountain”, the project’s fourth studio album, is now out via Icy Cold Records of France. It was mixed and post-produced by William Faith (Faith and the Muse, Christian Death, Mephisto Walz, Shadow Project, The March Violets) at 13 Studio in Chicago, and mixed and produced by Sven Wolff at Cosmonaut Studio in Berlin, with additional contributions from VV & the Void and Kill Shelter.

items.title: Dismantled: ‘Salvaging These Emotions into Something Called Music’
items.summary: Dismantled's Gary Zon talks to Side-Line about new album "Endless", out November 20, 2026 via Metropolis Records, 15 years after "The War Inside Me".
items.fullText:
Fifteen years after “The War Inside Me”, Gary Zon returns with “Endless”, the sixth studio album from Dismantled, scheduled for release on November 20, 2026, through Metropolis Records.

Since emerging in 2000, Dismantled has occupied a distinctive place in electro-industrial music. Zon’s compositions have always carried something deeply personal beneath their layers of distorted electronics, intricate programming and often abrasive arrangements. Albums such as “PostNuclear”, “Standard Issue” and “The War Inside Me” revealed an artist capable of translating frustration, alienation and emotional vulnerability into music of remarkable intensity, without entirely surrendering his sense of irony.

The road to “Endless” has been anything but straightforward. Side-Line first reported on the album in May 2020, and the record has taken years to reach completion, during a period in which Zon’s relationship with music, creativity and his own artistic identity continued to evolve. Side-Line covered the album’s slow re-emergence through the singles “Zero” in September 2026 and “Wired For War” later that same month, before the full November 20 release date was confirmed in October.

For Side-Line, Karo Kratochwil spoke with Gary Zon about the return of a project that, more than two decades after its beginnings, remains unmistakably his own.

Karo: Gary, you recently described Dismantled’s return as more of a “crawlback” than a proper comeback. That’s an interesting distinction, particularly from someone who once had such strong ambitions for the project. Fifteen years separate “The War Inside Me” and “Endless”, although you’ve continued releasing music in between. The new album was first announced in 2020, with previews appearing in 2021. What happened to your relationship with Dismantled during those years? And how much of the person who started this project in 2000 do you still recognise in yourself?

Gary Zon: Dismantled has always been a broken emotional outlet that I’ve come back to over the years because I couldn’t find anything else that worked better. Age and time definitely don’t help things either. But here I am, still doing an interview. I’ve reached a kind of obscurity with the project that reminds me of the way things used to be before I ever made music.

“The War Inside Me” was a great tumultuous period in my life that will always stay with me. But things don’t last, and time takes its toll. I had stomach surgery in 2012, and my energy hasn’t been the same since. I ended up back in the Northwest trying to complete the new album but struggled with finding myself again. After finally getting back on track, the pandemic hit.

I kept thinking I could get the album done quickly, like I did in my twenties. That was definitely not the case, and even though I kept posting previews and announcing it, the music wasn’t complete, and there was nothing I could do to speed up the process.

The energy in Oregon was horrible, and the years in pandemic isolation blended together until I lost track of time completely. I was too stubborn to give up, however, and kept grinding away at it. Moving back to California is the only thing that finally helped me finish the new album.

Karo: I have to ask you about “Exit”, because it’s genuinely one of my twenty favourite songs of all time. I’ve listened to an enormous amount of electronic music over the years, but very few compositions have affected me quite so profoundly. Even now, hearing it can feel almost like having my heart torn apart. What was happening in your creative life when you wrote it? And there’s something else I’ve noticed: from “Exit” through “No Escape” to “Mirror’s Edge”, the language of confinement and failed escape keeps returning. Are you still confronting essentially the same questions about freedom, or has their meaning changed over the years?

Gary Zon: Thank you for the compliment! “Exit” was the first song that I actually sang with clear vocals. The emotion at that time was me failing college and seeing society as a wall instead of something I could fit into. My only outlet to channel all that frustration ended up being that song. The lyric “whenever I feel / I find no way to begin” summed up my entire college experience. Going to classes every day unable to focus on anything while everyone around me seemed to thrive was how I wrote the entire “PostNuclear” album.

Years later, I heard from a fan of mine how listening to that album actually helped them finish college. That made me feel like all those wasted years at the University of Oregon were finally worth it.

And yes, I do feel the same way about “Exit” in the present day because I’m currently in the same dysfunctional atmosphere where society has become a wall that I can’t climb, but for much different reasons. I’ve come back to that feeling with the song “Mirror’s Edge” off “Endless”, which has elements of “Exit” but is channelled much differently.

Freedom has always been a tricky thing for me because the more I feel constricted emotionally, the better the music ends up being, at least in Dismantled’s case. “No Escape” was written as a gut reaction to the pandemic and the way that hope was “just a mirror” of ourselves. “Mirror’s Edge” continues that thought and looks at society as a broken mirror. “Before we kill each other blindly then say we’re not the virus, look in the mirror.”

The older I get, the more disillusioned I become with the definition of freedom. The values and things that people consider “freedom” in America are incredibly stressful and unattainable for most. “Our lives expendable, there’s nothing to believe” is another lyric from “Mirror’s Edge” that comes to mind.

Karo: The lyrics of “Endless” repeatedly return to conformity, surveillance, technological dependence and the erosion of individuality. In “Cloned”, obedience becomes a condition of belonging, while “Zero” and “Shelter” approach the disappearance of personal identity from more intimate perspectives. Are these primarily criticisms of the technological systems we’re creating, or of the human willingness to surrender autonomy in exchange for acceptance and security? Do you see any meaningful distinction between the two?

Gary Zon: I think technology has shaped society in ways that only science fiction novels could imagine, which I remember reading a lot in high school. “1984” and “Neuromancer” were the primary inspirations for my first album.

I still remember when the internet was something the general public was only curious about, compared to how it completely envelops and shapes our entire lives these days. “Nanowires run forever” from the new song “Zero” is a lyric that sums all that up for me.

I think most people have already surrendered themselves to AI and cloud computing, which is where the song title “Nano Cloud Warning” came from. Not to mention phones that warn you when the music is being played too loud. “Satellites trace each breath you’ll ever take, this is the end.”

Karo: In a 2010 interview, you spoke about instability as a source of inspiration and suggested that emotional stability could actually undermine your creativity. I’ve always found that idea fascinating, but also worth challenging. Do you still believe conflict and discomfort are necessary to produce convincing Dismantled music? Or has time taught you to access those emotions without needing to experience the circumstances that originally generated them?

Gary Zon: I don’t think anything has changed with my relationship between songwriting and personal life, but I do think it’s cooled off quite a bit because I’m obviously not in my twenties anymore, and that was the era when I wrote most of the albums.

Each of them has a colour theme that explains the emotions behind it. The self-titled is green since it’s all about the dystopian technology apocalypse. “PostNuclear” is orange-themed since that technology had begun to rust, becoming more organic and fragile.

“Standard Issue” was a very white-and-black, tongue-in-cheek album because that’s the way I felt like I was perceived in the industrial scene at the time. “The War Inside Me” was a red-and-black album that broke through all the confines of the previous albums in terms of emotional intensity.

“Endless” is blue-themed and combines all the previous album eras into something more complete and cohesive. It’s also the longest album I’ve ever written to make up for the delay in releasing it.

Karo: You’ve previously explained how the heavily processed, almost inhuman vocals of your debut gradually gave way to clearer singing because you wanted to communicate more personal emotions. Yet electronic manipulation can sometimes make vulnerability even more unsettling than an exposed human voice. How do you approach that balance today? And when working on “Endless”, did you find yourself returning to earlier production techniques for their emotional possibilities, rather than simply their association with the original Dismantled sound?

Gary Zon: I think I’ve found the balance between the vulnerable and heavily processed vocals on the new album in ways that I’ve never been able to achieve before. I’ve tried to blend them together with the music more, which is how the self-titled album sounded, at least in parts.

My favourite would have to be on the title track “Endless” because it’s all just vocoder but has so much emotion to me. That reminds me of the early days when I’d use a command-line program to make the vocals for “Dystopia”. That kind of experimentation is what I miss the most from those early days of creating music.

Karo: During the “Standard Issue” period, you were openly critical of the formulaic nature of industrial club music, while deliberately incorporating some of those conventions into your own compositions. You even seemed to enjoy the irony of audiences dancing to songs whose criticism they might completely miss. Does that contradiction still amuse you? With something as accessible as “Zero”, is it important that listeners understand the lyrics, or can misunderstanding become part of the artistic statement?

Gary Zon: I put a lot of thought into the lyrics, and that seems to be my weakness. Because I view the lyrics and the music as a complete picture, that ultimately affects the way I finish my songs.

So as soon as I hear another industrial track playing after my song on a playlist, the first thing I notice is how the music sounds much louder than mine, but the lyrics are more of an afterthought. That’s what I’ve come to expect over the years, however.

“Standard Issue” was an amazing era creatively, and there is still some of that lingering with the lyrics to “Zero”, but I think I’m content with just being ignored at this point. Irony and sarcasm are something that has sadly been lost to time and is no longer relevant in 2026.

Karo: In 2002, you described yourself as sceptical about politics and suggested that your music was more observational than activist. Yet “No Escape”, released in 2020, included an explicit call for climate action and supported Oregon wildfire relief. Now “Endless” returns to environmental destruction, technological control and humanity’s apparent inability to learn from its mistakes. Has your perspective changed? Do you still see music primarily as a way of documenting the human condition, or do you believe it can genuinely challenge the attitudes and behaviours it criticises?

Gary Zon: I believe music is at its lowest form of causing any sort of change since the dystopian corporatisation of the way artists are treated by companies like Spotify and Meta has sucked pretty much all soul out of trying to present anything unique and against the grain, in my opinion.

And yes, after the Oregon wildfires, I’ve definitely had a change of heart since it was right there in my community. When you can’t go outside for a week because you’re smoked in, and eventually the smoke starts coming into the house and you can’t breathe properly, you realise that climate change is right there in front of you, and yet nothing is being done about it.

I remember rendering the lyric video for “No Escape” just as the smoke rolled in. There was a particular campfire smell to it that made me feel like a kid again. Later that year, the fires reached California, and the entire West Coast looked like the scene from “Blade Runner 2049” when they’re in a future Las Vegas.

“The Fires Out West” reflects all those moments and is probably the most haunting song off the new album for me since I’ve personally experienced it.

Karo: You’ve explored music outside the industrial scene through projects such as Aerodrone and no.not.never, while also drawing inspiration from artists far removed from traditional electro-industrial music. Yet you’ve described Dismantled as the most direct expression of your personal relationship with the world. What is it about this particular musical language that allows you to communicate things you cannot express elsewhere? And after so many years, does the industrial scene still offer you creative possibilities, or do you sometimes find its conventions restrictive?

Gary Zon: Dismantled has always been a gut reaction to my environment that I come back to even though I consciously reject it.

“Endless” was the most difficult album I’ve ever worked on, and it took a lot of tries to finally get it to sound complete. It’s hard to explain except for the fact that the creation of sound and eventually recording vocals is the only way I feel fulfilled creatively and free to do other things.

I’ve started on the path of expressing myself through Dismantled long ago, and so it was only natural to finish what I started. My main goal, however, is just to show the hardcore fans that the music is very much still alive but is just taking that much longer to surface than before.

Karo: You’ve described “Endless” as your most cohesive album, and I can hear connections with different periods of your earlier work. But I also sense a change in the emotional language, particularly when comparing its more measured moments with the almost confrontational intensity of “PostNuclear” or “The War Inside Me”. Do you recognise that difference yourself? And how do you rediscover an earlier musical identity without turning it into something predictable? What does “Endless” express that the Gary Zon of twenty years ago might not have been capable of articulating?

Gary Zon: I was reading a lot of Victor Hugo during the writing of “Endless” because that’s how much my energy had dwindled being in Oregon, stuck in isolation from the pandemic. I love how his books are so epic in scope but have now become totally obscure relics that sit there collecting dust. I see a lot of myself in that energy, but even more obscure since I’ve never had much commercial success to begin with.

My favourite book by Victor Hugo turned out to be “The Toilers of the Sea”. In it, a protagonist salvages a shipwreck stuck on these two cliffs in the open sea all by himself. That reminded me of how I made all my albums, essentially just salvaging these emotions into something called music, no matter how much time it took or how broken it made me feel.

I’ve listened to a lot of the same bands while making “Endless” that I was listening to when I made “PostNuclear”, particularly Smashing Pumpkins and Radiohead. The new Silversun Pickups album was another source of inspiration.

I wanted to find a completeness to the sound that would sum up the project so when someone discovers my CD lying around collecting dust like an old Victor Hugo book, they can connect it back to my previous albums and see how it all fit together.

I’m much more fascinated with obscurity than achieving any form of success at this point. That ship has sailed and was never meant for the sort of thing I was doing anyway. In my early years, I always thought I was on the cusp of achieving something that never came.

That being said, I’m still proud of the work that I’ve accomplished over the years and excited to finally have an album done. It took a lot of willpower and determination to get to this point, as the years after the pandemic have been rough seas.

Karo: Finally, what about bringing Dismantled back to the stage? You always approached live performances rather differently from many electronic acts, insisting on the physical energy of a full band with live drums and bass. Is that still central to how you imagine Dismantled performing? Are there plans for concerts or perhaps another European tour? And looking beyond “Endless”, do you feel you’ve reopened a creative chapter that you want to continue exploring, or are you deliberately leaving the future of the project undefined?

Gary Zon: I still have amazing memories touring with the longest lineup I’ve had, which was TZA on keyboards and Jon Siren on drums. TZA sadly passed away in 2017, and a lot of grief from that is what makes “Endless” a very special album for me.

I miss her very much, and I’ve memorialised the lineup in the album artwork and added all the tours we did from that time period. This was the peak era of Dismantled live shows, especially with Nero Bellum joining on guitar, and will probably never be matched again.

That being said, I do want to visit Europe again in the future. Only time will tell.

About Dismantled

Dismantled is an American electro-industrial project founded by musician and producer Gary Zon in 2000. Emerging from experiments with layered electronic arrangements, distorted vocals and melodic synthesiser sequences, the project developed a recognisable sound combining electro-industrial aggression with atmospheric textures and deeply personal songwriting.

Following its self-titled debut in 2002, Dismantled released albums including “PostNuclear”, “Standard Issue” and “The War Inside Me”, establishing a catalogue that moved between dystopian electronic imagery, dark humour and increasingly direct emotional expression. Side-Line first reported on a follow-up album, “Endless”, in May 2020.

After a prolonged interval between studio albums, Dismantled returned to the singles chart with “Zero” in September 2026 and “Wired For War” later that month, ahead of its sixth full-length, “Endless”, set for release on November 20, 2026, through Metropolis Records. The twelve-track album includes both singles.

“Endless” is available for pre-order now on Bandcamp.
