items.fullText:
Kllsignl is a relatively new name on the Electro scene—a German solo project about which very little is known. Following the release of several singles, the label Out Of Line has now issued this EP, which combines familiar tracks with new material. Kllsignl sees itself as a manifestation: the embodiment of dark thoughts, sleepless nights, inner demons and psychological confrontations.

The five tracks are highly compelling, not least because Kllsignl’s musical style is difficult to pin down—a quality I have always considered a sign of genuine creativity. While the music could loosely be categorized as Dark-Electro, Industrial-Pop or even Industrial-Hip-Hop, its sound is distinctly its own. The production is overwhelming, at times resembling a form of ‘controlled chaos’, yet everything is meticulously crafted. Cold, stark textures are blended with a wealth of effects and anchored by powerful, driving beats. The vocals hover somewhere between singing and spoken word.

“Wendigo” is something you really need to discover for yourself. This project undoubtedly brings something fresh to the table. (Rating:7½).

Watch the clip “Wendigo”:

About Kllsignl

Kllsignl is a solo dark electro-trap project from Munich, Germany. The project signed to Berlin-based label Out Of Line and released its debut single and video “Wendigo” on May 8, 2025, followed the next day by its first live performance at the Out Of Line Weekender in Berlin. Side-Line first reported on the signing and the single at the time. All music, lyrics and production are credited to Kllsignl alone. The five-track “Wendigo” EP followed on Out Of Line in July 2026, combining the original single with four new tracks: “I Am The”, “Feed the Crows”, “Zero Me” and “Gimme That Kllsignl”.

items.title: István Gazdag interview: ‘Art and music don’t just play a role, they are the only thing that still makes me believe in humanity’
items.summary: István Gazdag is a Hungarian Electronic musician, producer, and composer who has been part of...
items.fullText:
István Gazdag is a Hungarian Electronic musician, producer, and composer who has been part of the underground Electronic music scene since the late 1980s. I have followed his work for years and have always been impressed by his main project, First Aid 4 Souls, in which he blends a variety of genres, ranging from Industrial and Dark-Electro to EBM. He is also involved in several other musical projects, including Stahlgeist, Vacuum X, and First Aid Tech. I suspect that few people are aware of the many prominent artists he has worked with over the years. This is a testament not only to his immense talent but also, and perhaps more importantly, to his remarkable instinct for sound, arrangements, and remixes. I often wonder whether he would have gained much wider recognition had he been based in a country with a more established Electronic music scene. His talent and creativity truly know no bounds. Yet beyond the musician lies an equally fascinating individual: someone with a sharp, clear-eyed perspective on our society and the complexities of human relationships and interactions. This interview goes beyond music, delving into his personal philosophy, his observations on the world around him, and the ideas that shape his artistic vision. What follows is an account of the conversation I had with him. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries)

István Gazdag interview

Q: István, what can you tell us about your musical background, and how did you first come into contact with underground Electronic music, which eventually led you to become the musician you are today?

István: I went to music school from primary school age, but I was never really good at anything. My mother took great care that my classical music education would be outstanding. By the end of the seventies, Kraftwerk fever had reached Hungary too, and these two strong influences marked my childhood. I got synthesizers from an uncle in America, made loops on crappy cassette tapes and played over them. Then in the mid-eighties Cabaret Voltaire and Yello came along, and around 1988 Skinny Puppy. The rest was a given.

Q: Over the years you’ve started quite a few projects. What does each one mean to you individually, and do you see them as different sides of the same artist, or rather as separate entities?

István: More like moods of the same eternally rebellious character. But the main line is First Aid 4 Souls; that’s where I’m true to myself.

Q: I understand Vacuum was your first project. What have you kept from those beginnings, and what has changed radically since then in your general approach to style, composing and production? And what is the difference for you today between Vacuum, Vacuum(X), First Aid 4 Souls, First Aid Tech and Stahlgeist?

István: Vacuum was the energetic experimentation of two crazy kids inspired by Cabaret Voltaire and Skinny Puppy. Technically, even back then I was far above the Hungarian average. I lent instruments to other Hungarian bands too, and never asked for anything in return. I still work with those instruments today. I can program the Ensoniq EPS 16 with my eyes closed… I think nothing has changed, except that I can mix my songs much more beautifully now. I still compose in a kind of Trance, completely shutting out the illusion that others experience as reality.

Vacuum is ancient Hungarian Dark-Electro/EBM, while Vacuum (X) has by now become a multi-disciplinary art project flirting with contemporary poetry. First Aid Tech is my more danceable side, Stahlgeist, currently on ice for a longer period, is the playground of my old-school EBM devotion, and First Aid 4 Souls is all of this at once, multiplied.

Q: Over the years you’ve worked with quite a lot of people, especially vocalists. Do you have specific criteria when choosing who to work with, and what have you learned from these collaborations?

István: I’ve worked with an incredible number of people and bands. The number of collaborations, public and non-public, is over 100, and truly on every continent. I’m always surprised by how professional they are. Seriously. I have a kind of confident arrogance, but the other artist’s astonishing talent always puts it in its place. What I’ve learned is that all the colors are there in the darkness, and that sensitive people often hide behind toughness.

Q: Do you need a particular mood or state of mind to make music for a given project, or how does that process work for you?

István: It’s very strange, but negative or tragic things make me angry, and anger breeds creativity. I think that’s why I still have my mind, and why I still have so much to say.

Q: Perhaps not everyone knows that you’ve made remixes for big names like Coil, Soft Cell, Test Dept., Cabaret Voltaire or Einstürzende Neubauten… How did these opportunities come about, and how did you approach making the remixes? Did you have personal contact with the artists, and did you get feedback from them?

István: I’m a member of the Some Bizzare family, and I was welcomed as one. The notorious Stevo, however self-willed he may be, is a good man deep down. At least to me. He paved my way, and through him I also got my membership in the UK Musicians’ Union (MU). And yes, I received feedback from the icons of my life. Test Department wrote that they would use my remix in the backing tracks for their concerts, and The Grid was also very appreciative. Recently there was talk of me being an active contributor to a secret Coil reissue as well.

Q: In an earlier interview you said that music must offer meaningful content and be able to fill a kind of inner emptiness. I find this interesting, especially considering the role and impact of art in a world burdened by conflict, alienation, division and the like. How do you see this, and what role does art, especially music, play in your own life?

István: In my intellectual life, art and music don’t just play a role, they are the only thing that still makes me believe in humanity. Without art, a human being is less than an animal.

Q: You seem like a very artistic person, and some of your music is connected to writers, paintings and other art forms. You had the chance to work on multidisciplinary projects where different art forms met so would you like to explore this in the future again, and if so, what would you imagine?

István: Oh, I can’t even list how many such projects I’ve been part of… Besides film and ballet scores, there were signature tunes for world championships, musical identities for global companies, title music for TV shows. I haven’t just explored it, I’ve been an active shaper of it. I’m also working right now on a segment of music, typography and contemporary Hungarian poetry, but let that remain a secret for a while.

Q: Dark and bleak themes have always been a kind of muse for scenes like EBM, Dark-Electro and Industrial. But today many of these dystopian themes have simply become reality. Do they still work as a kind of muse or fantasy, or have they perhaps evolved into a form of resistance?

István: This world can only be told truthfully in a whisper or a scream. Both sound good in these genres…

Q: In countries run by conservative or oppressive leaders, music and art are often closely watched or controlled. What was the situation in Hungary under Viktor Orbán’s rule, and have you noticed any change under the current government?

István: In Hungary, nobody persecuted artists who rebelled against the Orbán regime. They only threatened to. But they did everything, literally everything, to ruin them financially and isolate them mentally. This greatly raised the quality but reduced the reach.

Orbán and his rabble are a plague. Hungary was days away from a Belarusian nightmare. At this moment it is one of the most mentally and spiritually burned-out, financially completely plundered countries in Europe. This gave my best songs their ammunition. And I’d like to tell you something. I don’t follow any political direction. Anti-fascism has been a basic human minimum expectation since the Holocaust, but that doesn’t mean I’m a leftist. Anti-communism is an obvious human reaction for anyone born into a communist dictatorship (like me), but that doesn’t mean I’m a rightist. There is one important thing I can tell you: now that the capital-funded liberal elite has unleashed chaos on you, don’t think that the far-right response to it will help. It will bring hell down on your heads. I can say this because I have lived in both. I have made music in both.

Q: Back to music: what does your studio look like, and how has it evolved over the years alongside technological changes? And what is your opinion on the use of artificial intelligence in composing music?

István: I have a serious studio and a Jack Dangers-level sound bank (well, okay, half of it 🙂 ). You’d never believe it, but until a few years ago my workstation was a crappy old PC pulled out of a school’s junk clearance. You don’t need more for MIDI, and Nuendo 2 ran nicely on it 🙂 Now I have a serious computer, but I’m still surrounded by real ‘hardware’ instruments. I only work this way now. In fact, the new Vacuum X is largely a mix of EPS sequencer and live Osmose improvisation.

AI doesn’t bother me. It often helps me think through extremely difficult philosophical or social-science work. In music it’s of no use to me. I devoted a day to it and tried it. I can make better effects 🙂

Q: Do you have any special habits or rituals when you start working on a new song or album? Could you tell us a bit more about your working method?

István: My only ritual is this: when I first catch the theme, I give it everything and try to reach the maximum, and when I feel that this is good, this will last, I shoot the system down with a hard reset, without saving. It’s a burnt offering. The burning of the ego. Then the next day I play it again. There are many hundreds of these; often I finish them over many years.

Q: I find the latest First Aid Tech album, “Back To Agartha”, a very special production because of the many influences you blend together. I especially hear the influence of Juno Reactor; Ben Watkins is an absolute god to me. Could you tell us more about the album and the inspirations behind it?

István: Ben Watkins! I think I don’t need to say more 🙂 By the way, did you know that my Psy-Trance records have reached 10,000 direct downloads? Look up my FA4S albums “Navigator” or “Back To Shambala” on the Psy-Trance site Ektoplazm.

Q: Last year you released what might be the most surprising First Aid 4 Souls album yet, “Progenitrix”, especially because of the “Divas Of The Dark” contributions, a selection of female vocalists. How did the idea for this concept come about, and how did you put it together?

István: I wrote the album for my two little daughters, and I wanted serious, mature women to sing to them about the feelings of serious, mature women. I wrote it on ancient analog instruments and drum machines, and only after the vocal tracks were finished did the songs go into a modern studio, and even there I only added to them. The result turned out very authentic and refined. A true underground success album.

Q: Meanwhile, you this year released a new First Aid 4 Souls album as well. What would you like to say about the record “Totems In A Field Of Pain”?

István: ‘The Paradox of Liberation: From Pavlov to Foucault’.

One of the important starting points of the materialist picture of modern humans is the realization that a large part of our behavior stems from biological, psychological and social influences. Pavlov’s physiological research showed that there is a close connection between the nervous system and behavior: certain stimuli can trigger learnable reactions. Later behaviorism carried this thought further and increasingly interpreted human behavior as a conditionable system. The problem becomes truly interesting when we connect all this with the functioning of society.

Marx interpreted the human being primarily as a social being: our thinking and life possibilities are determined by material and social relations. Foucault, by comparison, examined how social institutions and discourses create categories by which a person is regarded as normal or abnormal, healthy or sick, acceptable or deviant.

One of Foucault’s most important insights is precisely that power does not work only through prohibition. It categorizes, observes, normalizes, and over time the individual begins to monitor themselves according to these norms. Here, however, a paradox appears.

What happens when new and newer identity categories are born from a philosophy of dismantling categories? Certain currents of contemporary identity politics, starting from Foucault’s ideas, rightly question the earlier, stigmatizing social categories. At the same time, liberation itself can also create new categories: new identities, new community boundaries, new moral hierarchies.

Thus a peculiar turn can occur: after the old categories are dismantled, new categories appear which over time can play just as strong an identity-defining role as those we originally wanted to dismantle.

‘Insofar as social progress depends on science, specialized ‘experts’ and uncontrollable market exchange relations, the propertyless, lay citizen (citoyen) necessarily loses his autonomy. The logic of progress artificially maintains the privileges of experts, while the lay masses become vulnerable in the process and lose their autonomy’. We can call this the paradox of liberation.

The question is not whether a formerly stigmatized identity deserves respect. Of course it does. The question is rather whether social acceptance necessarily goes hand in hand with the emergence of a new identity hierarchy.

A transgender person, for example, can be a fully autonomous and free individual, but a bodily or identity change in itself does not answer the philosophical question of freedom. Physiological change and existential freedom are not the same concept. Likewise, belonging to a sexual minority or another identity group does not automatically mean greater philosophical freedom.

This matters because we can easily confuse legal, social, bodily and philosophical freedom. But we can just as easily hollow out the concepts of morality, spirituality and love. If the human being appears primarily as the sum of categories, conditionings and power relations, then morality can become mere behavior regulation, spirituality psychological self-interpretation, and love a norm of acceptance. In such a system the question is no longer how we truly turn toward the other person, but whether we use the right language, recognize the right identity, and comply with the expectations of the given community.

Thus love, too, can lose its self-transcending character. Instead of seeing in it the one-time and irreplaceable person of the other, we may easily begin to love a representative of a category, or expect love on the basis of a category. Morality then is not the search for the good but the monitoring of normative compliance. Nor does spirituality necessarily remain a space of inner transformation, repentance, self-surrender or approach to truth, but becomes an identity-signaling and self-affirming practice.

This hollowing out is especially dangerous because from the outside it looks like liberation. The system rejects the old constraints but creates new ones in the process: it prescribes not what we should believe but how we should speak; not whom we should love but in what form we must express our love; not how we should live morally but which moral positions we must publicly represent.

The real philosophical question is deeper than this: can a person define themselves without becoming the prisoner of some ready-made identity category, and can they relate to the other in such a way that love is not mere social duty but genuine personal turning-toward?

This point also allows an interesting critique of Foucault’s own thinking. For if we examine every act of categorization as a form of power, then the new identity-political categorization itself should be subjected to the same critique.

Otherwise all that has happened is that the old normative system has been replaced by a new one, while behind the moral language the good has disappeared, behind spirituality transcendence, and behind love the real person of the other.

Art is an interesting counterexample to this. The artist is not simply the product of a social category. The creator is able to bring into being a form that did not exist before. Environment, biology, memory and social experience are of course all present in them, yet creation still brings forth new meaning.

The same question appears in conversion. Neurologically, brain processes, neuroplasticity, the rearrangement of memory and changes in emotional processing can be described. But describing them does not necessarily exhaust what a person experiences as conversion. The description of a nervous process is not necessarily identical to understanding the meaning of the event. Conversion is not merely the adoption of a new identity, but can also be the realization that a person does not draw their ultimate value from themselves, and that moral life is not merely adaptation to social expectations but a response to a truth and love greater than oneself.

Therefore, at the end of the path of thought leading from Pavlov to Foucault, perhaps the most important question is not whether ‘we are biorobots’.

But rather this: if a person truly lives among biological and social determinations, are they nevertheless able to reinterpret themselves, and are they able to find their way back to the true content of morality, spirituality and love?

If they are, then freedom does not necessarily mean the complete absence of determination. It may rather mean the ability to recognize our own conditioning, reflect on it, and, to a certain extent, give it a new direction. This new direction, however, cannot be exhausted by adopting a new identity. It must include responsibility, self-restraint, attention to the other, and also the possibility that a person not merely express themselves but also give themselves away.

In this sense, the artist, the philosopher and the convert may be three different manifestations of the same human possibility: not simply suffering what the world has made of them, but trying to create something new out of themselves, and in doing so rediscovering that the ultimate meaning of human freedom is not the limitlessness of self-definition, but free openness to truth, to the good, and to the other person.

Q: What else would you like to achieve, and above all create, as a musician? And what would be your ultimate dream?

István: There are still a few icons in my life whom I respect to the extreme. With them I’d like to make the second part of the duology, the male album. Names have said yes that even I can hardly believe. My ultimate dream? To wake up.

About István Gazdag

István Gazdag is a Hungarian Electronic musician, producer and composer based in Budapest. He started out in the mid-1980s with Vacuum, a Dark-Electro/EBM project influenced by Cabaret Voltaire, Yello and Skinny Puppy. Vacuum later evolved into Vacuum (X), a multi-disciplinary project that combines electronic composition with contemporary poetry.

Gazdag’s main outlet is First Aid 4 Souls, blending Industrial, Dark-Electro and EBM. The project signed to Belgian label Alfa Matrix in August 2019 with a label-debut EP, followed by the album “Keep This World Empty”. “Fire”, released in June 2020, paid tribute to the Hungarian subculture community LD50.hu, and the “Dreambox” EP followed that October. The album “I Am The Night” arrived in May 2022, and 2023 brought the EP/mini-album “Dancing At The Abyss”, the EP “Laudator Temporis Acti” and the 70-track back-catalogue compilation “This Present Darkness”.

In December 2025, First Aid 4 Souls released the post-punk and darkwave-leaning album “Progenitrix”, built around a cast of guest female vocalists the project calls “Divas Of The Dark”. The latest First Aid 4 Souls album, “Totems In A Field Of Pain”, followed via Alfa Matrix on 26 June 2026.

Gazdag also records as First Aid Tech, a more dance-oriented outlet that released its debut EP in December 2023, and as Stahlgeist, an old-school EBM project that signed to Alfa Matrix in October 2022 with an alternate version of the album “Escape Reality”; Stahlgeist is currently on hold. Beyond his own projects, Gazdag has remixed material for Coil, Soft Cell, Test Dept., Cabaret Voltaire and Einstürzende Neubauten as a member of the Some Bizzare roster and the UK Musicians’ Union.

Side-Line has interviewed Gazdag’s projects several times, including a 2020 Click Interview with First Aid 4 Souls, a 2022 Click Interview, a First Aid 4 Souls interview in March 2026, a 2023 interview with Stahlgeist and a 2025 interview with First Aid Tech. This latest conversation, courtesy of Inferno Sound Diaries, moves beyond the music to cover Gazdag’s outlook on art, artificial intelligence and Hungary under Viktor Orbán.

items.fullText:
Mia Van Wyk and Paul Gala make up the South African duo Hunter As A Horse. Following several previous releases, primarily singles, the band now makes a strong comeback with the support of the label Metropolis Records. The arrival of this 12-track album was preceded by several singles. The songs largely explore personal experiences centred on the human condition, suggesting that the darker side of an individual need not always be viewed in a negative light.

Musically, the project draws on a variety of influences, landing somewhere between Dream-Pop, Trip-Hop and Electro-Wave. The result is a distinctive production in which Mia Van Wyk’s unique, soft and remarkably fragile voice takes the listener by the hand, guiding them through her own personal universe. The music is imbued with melancholy and a strong sense of dreaminess. While most tracks have a gentle character, there are also a few sharper, harder-edged moments that provide a striking contrast. The music is occasionally enriched by acoustic-sounding instruments, although I suspect these may actually be synthesised textures. Either way, they add an extra artistic dimension to the overall sound. Finally, I must give a special recommendation to the title track, which is an absolute gem.

Hunter As A Horse certainly has a lot to offer, both in terms of style and execution. This is a beautiful album. (Rating:8).

Listen to “Paradise Lost”:

About Hunter As a Horse

“Always greet a ghost with a handkerchief, otherwise it will leave a black mark on your hand.” So said the grandmother of Mia Van Wyk who, after experiencing a family tragedy on a rural farm in South Africa’s Free State, took to writing songs and playing the guitar “only because I didn’t know what else to do with death.”

Hunter As a Horse began in the early 2010s as a duo formed in London by South African vocalist and guitarist Mia van Wyk and producer Paul Gala, who handled piano, synths and machines. The pair relocated from London to Berlin and later undertook a year-long self-imposed exile in rural Italy, writing material.

The first substantial release under the name was the EP “The Two Magics Vol.1”, issued digitally in April 2016 via Valley Of Fire Recordings. The five-track release, featuring songs such as “The Passenger”, “Dead Stars”, “The Abyss”, “Fallen Leaves” and “A Million Julys”, brought a blend of synth-driven storytelling and indietronica. A second release, “The Two Magics Vol.2”, followed in July 2017.

In parallel with these EPs, individual Hunter As a Horse songs were used in television and media. The track “The Passenger” appeared in the pilot episode of the US series Riverdale, with further use in American Horror Story, Mercedes Benz commercials, the trailer for Wander Darkly and episodes of the Netflix series Elite.

After a period of relative quiet, Hunter As a Horse returned in 2019 with the four-track EP “Walk With Fire”, followed in August 2023 by the 8-track “The Lost Tapes EP” on Bad Future Records, a Johannesburg-based label co-founded to handle the project’s releases. In 2025 came the six-track EP “ANATHEMA”, issued on 11 April via Bad Future and distributed by Ditto Music, followed by the full-length “VISIONS” (deluxe) LP combining tracks from that EP with related sessions.

Mia van Wyk signed with Metropolis Records to release “Lighthouse” in January 2026, followed in March by “Here’s To All The Ones”, and now continues with the twelve-track album “Paradise Lost”, also for Metropolis.

items.fullText:
Two faces, Heals by day, Breaks by night
Morning comes, mask erased

By day, the kitchen window gives you the street. Switch on the light after dark and your own face appears where the street was, still wearing the expression you’ve used to put other people at ease. The woman who appears in the title track of 2Faces, the second album by Belgian-Spanish darkwave duo Bella Eterna, knows that change in the light. She heals by day and breaks by night. Gerd Van Geel drops to a murmur for “By day, she paints. By night, she falls.” The smiles she paints in daylight keep her hurt out of sight. After dark, her composure gives way, and she feels the weight of what she’s spent the day covering up.

The title also refers to the two faces Domingo J. Casas photographed for the sleeve. Van Geel, the voice of Belgium’s The Arch, wrote the lyrics and sings throughout, while JG Outsider, the Spanish producer also known as Javi Golo, composed, programmed, and mixed the album. They credit 2Faces with the way each sparked new ideas in the other. For Outsider, who came up in Spanish clubs, the project was a way back to the ’80s electronics and goth that first made him want to make records. There’s more room for guitar and bass this time, and you can hear the two working as one when a bass line keeps its footing, and Van Geel lets one of his characters lose theirs.

And the night has its own myriad performances from its cast strewn across the songs of 2Faces. In one, a woman traces every step in a ballroom that’s beginning to feel like a cage. In another, a clown puts on a frightening face, yet gives himself away with the teddy bear clutched in his hand. Van Geel’s characters keep looking for a way out of the parts they’ve learned, whether that means burning the fairytale they were given or admitting what they still want. And the album’s first song asks what happens if a grown man decides he’s spent long enough acting his age.

“When I Grow Up,” the opener and lead single, begins with a bell-like figure, its rough edge hinting at guitar before reverb blurs it into something harder to name. As the drums arrive, Van Geel’s wordless cry slips into a growl, then settles into a croon with Gary Numan’s chilly poise. A rippling synth pattern keeps the song in motion while guitar notes thread through the spaces around his voice. He sings of wanting to laugh after dark and chase thunder through a world of “concrete dreams,” where there’s always a deadline pulling him back. The line “When I grow up, I want to be a child” places childhood just ahead of him, still within reach even after that choice has seemingly slipped away. The chorus rises with the abandon of someone who has already run out into the rain.

Van Geel sets the song’s video in a circus, where grown-ups make play look like work. A boy in a bowler keeps red balls aloft; a stilt walker in striped trousers looms above the troupe; a hoop spins as its performer lowers herself into a split. The clown’s painted smile remains fixed, though his eyes have already surrendered. At one point, he is rigged like a marionette, foreshadowing the dancer in the next song. In the final wide shot, he stands alone beneath the red-and-gold drapery, arms spread toward rows of empty seats.

Watch the video for “When I Grow Up” below.

The synth pads on “Break the Cage” exhale a Baroque melody, conjuring a ballroom scented with hot wax, flowers, and wine still lingering on someone’s breath. Beneath Van Geel, a supple synth bass glides as the woman in his song takes the floor, each marionette-precise step shadowed by a soul in debt. The arrangement could score the scene in Ridley Scott’s Legend where Princess Lili merges with her black gown, the rapture of the dance helping keep her ensnared. By the time Van Geel sings, “Burn the fairytale, break the cage,” the story that trapped her is the first thing she’s ready to set aflame.

On “2Faces,” a booming kick and snare dissolve into the bright sizzle of hi-hat and a scatter of handclaps. Van Geel stretches each vowel across a cool, crystalline guitar line, then sinks to a murmur as the Joker calls. A touch of Gotham enters the life of a woman who spends her days painting over cracks. Both faces wear the “Same disguise”—perhaps even the devil’s grin is just another expression she has learned to put on. When Van Geel’s voice rises again on “Lipstick, lies and gold,” you can almost see her preparing to face the room.

Low guitar tones give the synth melody in “Magic Tree” the hush and contour of a nocturne. Outsider lets the beat dissolve, then quietly restores it with a synth bass beneath Van Geel’s account of a body surrendering to the earth. First the legs go numb; soon, twigs are pushing through a human skull. Van Geel delivers the rising refrain with such composure that the bargain feels almost reasonable. The body that once could run can, at last, remain. By the time he calls himself the tree, he sounds almost at home.

In “Pink Teddy,” a clown lies beside a staged crime scene, clutching a toy bear. Outsider lends the tableau the menace of early Skinny Puppy, driven by an EBM bass sequence, low-slung synth notes, and eerie chimes. Van Geel begins submerged in reverb, then steps into the foreground with the clipped cadence of Al Jourgensen-era Ministry. The scene unfolds with the crooked logic of a Legendary Pink Dots fable—until Van Geel sings “He wanted love,” opening into a melody made for a roomful of voices. The bear remains a child’s thing in the hands of a man who has gone to considerable lengths to look frightening.

A metallic bass synth ricochets against the kickdrum on “Ballet for Sea Gods” as Van Geel sends his dancers plunging past teeth and scales. He begins with the air of someone recounting a tale handed down through generations. Then the drums crash into the refrain, and his voice gathers force until you can feel the dancers’ debt to the gods below. They dance to keep them asleep; every breath is part of the price. The tides alone bear witness.

The guitar riff on “Burn” retains its icy edge as the synths swell and the drums press in. A few notes echo Van Geel’s voice as he sings of a half-spider creature spinning a kingdom for itself in the swamp. His voice rises on “A thousand hungers burn inside,” before the chorus urges the creature to rise and fight. It already rules the mire on shattered knees—a detail that lends the command a cost. The record opened with the freedom of running out into the rain. By the end of its original tracks, simply getting to your feet in the mud demands everything you have.

After the incandescent “Burn,” David Kano and Juanjo Reig return to the album’s opening track with their “When I Grow Up” (Cycle Remix). This pared-back post-punk reprise rekindles the promise of a childhood not yet outgrown—and offers a welcome reprieve.

The final slot goes to “2Faces” (Parissior Remix), recast as ’90s-inspired electronica. The lead single and title track both return in fresh disguises, delivering one last twist on the album’s central idea: even a familiar face can still surprise.

2Faces is a perfect darkwave record, with dark synth-pop choruses that make you want to sing at full volume about the things people spend all day hiding.

The album is available digitally and on limited black vinyl through Mots Music. Listen to 2Faces below and order it here

Gerd Van Geel, also known as CUVG, started behind the drums in The Arch, the Belgian band formed in Breendonk in 1986. Producer Ludo Camberlin had the members try the vocal parts in the studio, and Van Geel wound up as the lead singer. The band’s 1990 track “Ribdancer” became a cult favorite in Spain. Van Geel also works behind the camera, directing Bella Eterna’s video for “Mysterious Beauty” from the Fire EP.

JG Outsider is Javier Gómez, the Alicante-born, Murcia-based DJ and producer also known as Javi Golo. He began DJing in 1984 and producing for Pink Records in 1992, then co-founded Essential, a label focused on vocal and progressive trance. His work as JG Outsider took him back to the EBM and industrial music that drew him in as a young DJ, territory he explored on his 2024 album Despierto for Cold Transmission.

Bella Eterna grew out of two reworkings of songs by The Arch. Outsider remixed “Phantom Chase” in 2020, then revisited “Ribdancer” for a Banshees Records tribute in 2023. The pair began writing together between Belgium and Spain, releasing their debut album Pornographic Shadows through Unknown Pleasures Records in 2024. Strictly Tempo put out Fire the following year, with Alpha Sect’s remix of “Me and the Desert”.

items.title: Richard Lloyd, Founding Member and Guitarist of Television, Passes Away at 75
items.summary: Richard Lloyd, the Television co-founder whose wiry leads made Marquee Moon a blueprint for generations of post-punk guitarists, died on Saturday, November 7, at his home in Chattanooga, Tennessee. He… The post Richard Lloyd, Founding Member and Guitarist of T
items.fullText:
Richard Lloyd, the Television co-founder whose wiry leads made Marquee Moon a blueprint for generations of post-punk guitarists, died on Saturday, November 7, at his home in Chattanooga, Tennessee. He was 75. His family said the cause was cholangiocarcinoma, a form of bile duct cancer diagnosed in March. “His loving wife Sheila and his dog Willie Mays were with him at the end,” the family said in a statement to Rolling Stone.

On “Marquee Moon,” Tom Verlaine starts with a repeating chord figure. Lloyd comes in against it, picking out two notes at a time, and Fred Smith’s bass and Billy Ficca’s drums enter in turn. Each part changes the way you hear the one before it. Lloyd takes the first solo after the second chorus, squeezes a few sharp bends into a short break, and gives the song back to the singer. Verlaine stretches out after the next chorus.

Lloyd’s ear for where a guitar should answer a singer served him well with Matthew Sweet. On Girlfriend (1991), he played the solos on “Divine Intervention” and “Evangeline.” Sweet recalled that the two took turns with the same Jazzmaster on “Evangeline,” with Sweet playing the recurring figure and Lloyd answering it before taking the solo. Lloyd returned for Altered Beast and 100% Fun. He also played on Meet John Doe, the solo debut of X’s bassist and singer.

Lloyd returned to Television for its self-titled third album in 1992 and played with the band on and off until leaving in 2007. Two years later he released The Jamie Neverts Story, an album of Hendrix covers that paid tribute to both Hendrix and Turner. He published his memoir, Everything Is Combustible, in 2017 and released The Countdown the following year.

At Baker Falls in New York City on January 23, 2026, the Richard Lloyd Group played “Alchemy” alongside Television’s “Elevation” and “Friction.” Lloyd had left the old band’s songs out of his sets for years. He spoke to Guitar World that January about what he’d set out to do with Television. “I wanted to make a dent in rock history. That was my goal, and that came true.”

Lloyd’s survivors include his wife, Sheila O’Keefe, and his son, Dylan.

items.fullText:
Philippe Münch continues to release an incredible volume of material. Whether through his well-established sonic alter egos, such as Synapscape and The Rorschach Garden, or through various other projects and collaborations, he also consistently produces a vast amount of work under his own name.

With “Krankpop”, he presents six tracks that effectively make up a mini-album. Working under his own name, he seems more inclined to experiment with different genres, free from the specific stylistic boundaries that define his aforementioned projects. As Philippe Münch, he is no longer bound by rigid expectations, allowing him to explore a much wider range of possibilities. The record opens with a Krautrock-inspired track, followed by what feels like an imaginary fusion of Cabaret Voltaire and Suicide. From there, he ventures further into experimentation, incorporating Industrial-leaning elements driven by powerful rhythms. The work unfolds like a book divided into distinct chapters, each clearly defined yet contributing to a coherent overall narrative.

While this isn’t my favourite release from this German veteran, it nevertheless contains several strong tracks. (Rating:7½).

Listen to “Train Crash”:

About Philipp Münch

Philipp Münch is a German electronic musician based in Bielefeld whose work spans industrial, rhythmic noise and electro. He founded The Rorschach Garden in 1988 and co-founded Ars Moriendi in 1989. In 1994 he formed Synapscape, the rhythmic-noise duo with Tim Kniep that debuted on Ant-Zen in 1995, and Mandelbrot. He began releasing solo albums in 2011, including “Greyscale” (2018) and “Tales From The Lower Cave” (2025), both on Ant-Zen. Ant-Zen, founded in 1993 in Lappersdorf, Germany, remains a reference point for industrial and power-noise music, and “Krankpop” reunites Münch with Babsi Teichner on a mini-album the label calls “brooding angstpop,” with “Train Crash” among its six tracks.

items.title: Welcome to Creepsville — NYC Horror Punks The Brickbats Unearth Lost Album “Let the Goodtimes Rot”

items.fullText:
By the mid-’90s, goth had enjoyed about as much daylight as it could stand. Interview with the Vampire made box-office bloodsuckers of Tom Cruise and Brad Pitt in 1994, and The Cure’s “Burn” opened the chart-topping soundtrack to The Crow. But by 1997, Saturday Night Live was sending up the scene with Goth Talk, a mock cable-access show that summoned the forces of darkness from the family couch.

The clubs were changing, too. At the Bank in New York, Ward 6 had already made room for industrial and EBM upstairs, with goth rock and post-punk holding down the floor below. By the end of the decade, some Los Angeles nights had pushed that crossover into techno and rave tempos. The apocalypse had acquired glowsticks and a programmable kick drum, and a whole generation of baby bats began to forget Goth’s punk roots.

But The Brickbats never forgot. The band started playing New York in 1995 with the Cramps’ rockabilly twitch, the Misfits’ gift for a gang chorus, and the Damned’s relish for a grand entrance. They brought garage-band velocity to goth nights and treated Halloween as a year-round booking, a combination that put them ahead of the early-2000s deathrock revival.  And by the time the first Drop Dead Festival came to CBGBs in 2003, singer and guitarist Corey Gorey and drummer DW Friend were on the bill with their next band, The Brides.

Gorey, Friend, and bassist Paul Morden recorded their long-lost fourth album, Let the Goodtimes Rot, with Jacques Cohen at The Space in Poughkeepsie, New York, in May and June 1999. But the record sat unfinished after the trio went on hiatus around 2000 when bassist Paul Morden headed to California to play with Gitane DeMone. Friend and Gorey salvaged the deteriorating reels and completed the songs; Gorey mixed the record, and Jeremy Hayes mastered it for its November 6, 2026 release. Twenty-seven years later, it still sounds impatient. The trio gets through thirteen songs in just over twenty-five minutes, changing pace every time you think you’ve got the measure of them.

DW Friend tumbles into the album’s title track, Let the Goodtimes Rot, with a drum fill, and Corey Gorey rakes out a jagged riff with one heel planted in old rock ’n’ roll. The refrain makes a whole-room singalong out of ejecting the guest who’s been killing the mood. Then spring-loaded guitar sets up Apt. of the Werewolf, and the bass and drums come crashing in. Gorey starts out sounding almost neighborly, then his words come quicker and give way to a howl. The rent is low enough to justify budgeting for silver ammunition. And New Yorkers have signed worse leases.

The kick drum knocks its way into Goosebumps, where a blues guitar answers Gorey’s gravelly honky-tonk drawl. The suitor offers his sweetheart a freshly extracted eyeball, then has to keep track of it when it rolls away. The guitar thickens into a steady chug and drops back into its easy swing, as if this were a perfectly ordinary second date. Friend’s next opening fill sends Too Bad Yuh Gonna Die straight into a crash of guitar, with Gorey delivering the bad news like an undertaker who’s already running behind. The refrain comes around too fast to give anyone time to argue.

On Reverb Vamplifier, the guitar tears through a surf riff, the drums keep up a merciless stomp, and the vocal melody has the lift of classic rockabilly. An icy guitar figure and a wash of keys briefly interrupt the charge, as if the secondhand amp in the song has started to act up. Its knobs are made from bones, and it houses the ghost of a roadie who died fetching Elvis a drink. The repair shop is going to have questions.

Gorey gives the King’s vowels an affectionate workout on Orange Shades, and the trio turns the bounce of “Blue Suede Shoes” into a full-tilt punk charge. The indignation over a $3.50 pair of sunglasses has the force of a man defending the deed to Graceland. More Red Wine eases into a surf saunter, with a touch of Dave Vanian’s poise circa “Eloise” in Gorey’s baritone. The song follows a woman tangoing through the small hours on Delancey Street. An altercation between her heel and a bottle of port does little to slow her down. The musicians give out first.

Friend’s opening toms summon Rock and Roll Ghost-A-Go-Go Show (Show), a Friday-night invitation to raise the dead for a three-chord set. Gorey rattles off the verses, and the chorus comes back with the weight of an Oi! gang chant. Then Theme from Frankenstein’s Hangover staggers through a bluesy surf riff like Herman Munster attempting the stairs. The beat keeps losing its footing, the guitar slides down the frets, and the monster groans as if someone has just switched on the overhead light.

The apparent hair of the dog for a monster hangover is Boozecan, where metallic percussion and clipped guitar sound like a rhythm section assembled from the empties. Gorey growls through an inventory of whiskey with a Tom Waits rasp, and the chorus takes on the swing of the Pogues as the drinkers move on to the next bar and leave the bill to management. The guitars chime over a hard, quick drumbeat on Rattle My Chains, and Gorey gives the poltergeist one of the album’s sweetest melodies. He sings the threats like a come-on. And all of a sudden, the Ouija board sounds like a singles hot line.

Creepsville takes the long way home. Gorey starts it with a gentle guitar figure that has some of the Doors’ slow, gothic sway and a curious kinship with what Interpol would play a few years later on “Leif Erikson.” The guitar syncs with Morden’s bass accentuations, leaving Gorey room to greet the town’s visitors by name and give them driving directions that end with their eyes shut. By the time the guitars bear down, the place is starting to feel like the setting of a Shangri-Las death disc or Hot Chocolate’s “Emma.” Giving the town four minutes to introduce itself lets the joke curdle into genuine unease. It’s the finest bit of pacing on the record.

We Gotta Go settles things in under a minute. A burst of Misfits-speed rockabilly finds the bartender running out of patience and daylight doing wonders for everyone’s decision-making. For a record that took twenty-seven years to get through the door, Let the Goodtimes Rot knows exactly how to make an exit.

Let the Goodtimes Rot is out now digitally and on limited-edition 12-inch vinyl. Order the album here.

The Brickbats’ original run yielded Sing You Dead, Creepy Crawly – The Unauthorized Autobiography of Undead Rock and Roll Music, and Monster Party. During the hiatus, Gorey and Friend formed The Brides with bassist Gregjaw and keyboardist Julia Ghoulia. After Morden’s death in 2006, the two returned to the stage as The Brickbats for a pair of shows in his memory in 2013, with Jason Trioxin on bass. Return of the Living Brickbats followed in 2016.

After Trioxin’s death, Gregjaw took over on bass and continued recording with the band until his death in January 2026. Gorey and Friend now work as a duo, using a rewired guitar setup to cover the low end as they write new material and prepare further catalog reissues.

items.title: “Release Me From This Web” — Ethereal Darkwave Duo Feyleux Examines the Dark Half of Self on “Shadeweaver”
items.summary: You can spend years thinking of yourself as easygoing before it occurs to you how much effort it takes to swallow your anger. Swallow it often enough and eventually it’s… The post “Release Me From This Web” — Ethereal Darkwave Duo Feyleux Examines the Dark Hal
items.fullText:
You can spend years thinking of yourself as easygoing before it occurs to you how much effort it takes to swallow your anger. Swallow it often enough and eventually it’s the anger that feels out of character, even when you have every reason to be furious. Carl Jung called the parts of ourselves we have trouble recognizing or accepting the shadow. It can hold envy and resentment, but it can also hold an appetite for attention, a talent we were taught to downplay, or the nerve to say when we’ve had enough. Bringing those parts into view means asking how much of what we call our personality began as a way to get along.

On Shadeweaver, Feyleux put that question to a beat you can dance to. Written largely in the winter of 2025–26, their second album for Swiss Dark Nights pairs Laurie Ruroden’s suspended vocal melodies with the bass, guitar, and drum programming that Erica Mauve Gilstrap keeps in motion underneath. That interplay takes shape immediately on “Remote Control.” A kick drum, a melodic synth figure, and a bass pulse set the pace. A guitar note hangs in the air as Ruroden sings about the cost of keeping quiet in a relationship. Early on, she pictures someone stranded out there alone. By the final chorus, the song has found a “we,” and the same beat that drew you in starts to sound like two people making for the door.

The urge to get away carries into “Frailty,” where Ruroden sings about howling at the world one moment and keeping safely out of sight the next. Little shivers of synth pass over soft pads, and the guitar cuts a clean line through them. It’s easy to imagine She Past Away making dream pop and keeping the beat that makes their records so easy to move to. After two songs that draw you in through rhythm, “Grave Moss” eases off the pace. Chiming keys and sighing pads give way to a romantic guitar jangle, with a warm bass melody low in the mix. Ruroden keeps asking whether someone has already passed beyond the veil. At this tempo, you hear the gap between the question and the moment she has to ask it again.

Water offers a hiding place on “Flutter + Fade,” though the metallic gothic-rock bass and firm kick give the reunion an uneasy footing. Icy keys gather above them, then the guitar starts to jangle and Ruroden’s voice lifts through the arrangement. She asks to meet somewhere private, where time stands still, before wondering how much longer the charade can go on. “Detachment” follows with a clean break set to surprisingly tender music. Dreamy synth tones give way to a higher, wavering line, and the vocal has the effect of a duet in places. As the synth and vocal melodies trade prominence, there’s room to hear some wistfulness in the delivery, even when Ruroden’s words leave little room for negotiation.

That sense of resolve gives way to a plunge on “Oubliette.” The opening guitar tones recall The Cure, clear and cold against the sigh of the synths. A sustained bass note and a rippling synth-bass figure bring in the darker vocal, and the arrangement rises and recedes like waves in a subterranean ocean. Even the name of the dungeon carries the threat of being forgotten, which makes the final twist especially sharp. Someone still remembers who’s down there. “Solitary World” takes that isolation in a different direction. It comes straight in with a dark synth-bass beat, and guitar and keys trade figures beneath the ethereal vocal. The chorus gives solitude two meanings at once. You’re left alone with a mind that plays tricks on you, and you get to decide what to do with the power you’ve taken back.

A low, muttering growl and a synth that rolls through the intro like a muffled siren make “Astral Weaver” sound ominous for a few seconds. Then a buoyant drumbeat and bass rhythm take over, and the guitar flutters with the lightness of early Cocteau Twins. The music makes the dream inviting enough that you can see why someone might stay there until it gets hard to leave. “Strawberry Moon” brings that tension out into the open with synth bass, a bright keyboard figure, and a burst of darkwave guitar. Bass guitar settles into a steady pattern as delayed notes skip under one of Ruroden’s catchiest melodies. Where the couple on “Remote Control” danced to get away, the lovers here have slipped away so they can dance together. You can still hear the danger in the guitar, but every return to the chorus makes their night feel a little more like their own.

Shadeweaver is out now via Swiss Dark Nights. Listen below, and order the album here.

Feyleux formed in mid-2023, with Laurie Ruroden on vocals and synths and Erica Mauve Gilstrap on guitar, bass, synths, and programming. The duo released their debut album, Midnight Hearts, through Swiss Dark Nights in 2024 and have since played more than a hundred shows. On their second album, Shadeweaver, they build on the debut’s blend of dream pop and darkwave, bringing ’80s new wave melodies into songs about grief, survival, and the parts of ourselves we learn to hide.

items.summary: What have you awakened? Cuz I’m already already gone Sometimes you catch yourself talking about a place in the past tense while you’re still sitting in it. Your coat is… The post “What Have You Awakened?” — Madison Darkwave Artist Carrellee Shares Video for “W
items.fullText:
What have you awakened?
Cuz I’m already already gone

Sometimes you catch yourself talking about a place in the past tense while you’re still sitting in it. Your coat is on the hook and the sunlight falls across the wall at its usual hour, but you’ve rehearsed leaving so often that the room has begun to feel like a memory. In Waiting, Madison, Wisconsin darkwave artist Carrellee weighs the time she’s lost to worry against the risk of putting her heart on the line again. She asks what someone has awakened in her and hears herself answer that she’s already gone. The second “already” sounds like the moment she realizes she means it.

The bass is already moving when she starts to sing. A springy synth figure doubles back on itself before the kick lands, and rippling synths gather behind her as bell tones ring between lines. Carrellee keeps her voice close, with the silky composure of Curve’s Toni Halliday and some of the frank sensuality of Sinéad O’Connor’s “I Want Your (Hands on Me).” The synth layers have the glossy sweep of Madonna’s Ray of Light.

Carrellee made that turn toward late-’90s and early-’00s techno and dance pop in Madison, where she wrote, performed, and produced the single. She brought back Maurizio Baggio (The Soft Moon, Boy Harsher) to mix and Josh Bonati (Adrianne Lenker) to master. Both worked on her self-titled 2025 album for Young & Cold Records.

Carrellee shot and directed the video herself, too, giving it the close framing and everyday details of a home movie. She lies among fallen leaves, sings beside a backyard grill with the wind pushing her hair across her eyes, and stretches her arms wide in front of shelves packed with records. By the water, the sun turns her into a silhouette. When the camera returns to the leaves, the ground is empty, as though the image has finally caught up with the refrain.

Watch the video for “Waiting” below.

Carrellee spent years performing as a folk artist before she turned to darkwave. Her 2022 debut, Scale of Dreams, sold out its first pressing on Negative Gain Productions, and No Coast Records put it back in print. She took those songs to Chicago’s Cold Waves, Vancouver’s Verboden, and a Synthicide night at Brooklyn’s Saint Vitus. On Rescaled, she handed them over to remixers including Patriarchy, Casket Cassette, and former Smashing Pumpkins guitarist Jeff Schroeder.

Touring brought her to IAMX, first as an opener in the Midwest in 2023 and then as a backing vocalist and synth player on European and North American dates in 2024 and 2025. Back in the studio, she brought in Matia Simovich and Ryan McCambridge for additional production on her self-titled second album. The record gave her a breakout single in “Captain,” earned airplay on KEXP, and reached the top ten of the Deutsche Alternative Charts. IAMX, INHALT, and Bragolin later reworked songs from it for a remix EP.

In 2026, Carrellee headlined a 30-date U.S. tour and returned to Verboden. Her collaboration with Bragolin extended beyond the remix. She sang on “Feel This Flame Unfold” from the Dutch darkwave project’s I Don’t Like What It Does to Me, and the labelmates co-headlined a North American run this fall. Carrellee will open for Bragolin on all 21 dates of their next run, which starts November 12 at Glasgow’s Ivory Blacks and marks her first European tour under the Carrellee name.

items.title: Mari Kattman releases new single ‘It’s In The Losing You’ via Metropolis Records
items.summary: US musician Mari Kattman releases "It's In The Losing You" via Metropolis Records on November 6, 2026, following her 2025 album "Year Of The Katt".
items.fullText:
US electronic musician and vocalist Mari Kattman has released her new single, “It’s In The Losing You”, today, November 6, 2026, through Metropolis Records.

Written and produced by Kattman herself, the track combines synth-pop, EBM and industrial influences with driving electronic beats and her distinctive vocals. Lyrically, it deals with self-worth, letting go of expectations and finally refusing to seek validation from others.

Kattman explains the idea behind the song:

“It’s about the liberation that comes with finally saying fuck it and realising that the validation you’ve spent a lifetime seeking was never someone else’s to give. Your worth is determined by the one constant – yourself.”

The single follows her 2025 album “Year Of The Katt”, her first full-length release for Metropolis Records. The album featured tracks such as “Anemia”, “Sharp Shooter” and “Typical Girl”.

Active as a musician, songwriter and producer since 2012, Kattman has built an extensive list of collaborations, including work with Mesh, Rotersand, Neuroticfish, Comaduster and Caustic.

More recently, she contributed vocals to “Ich Will Nur Das”, a September 2026 single by Lords Of Acid, released ahead of their album “Mundo Bizarro”.

Kattman has also been confirmed for the 2027 edition of M’era Luna Festival in Hildesheim, Germany.

“It’s In The Losing You” is available now on streaming platforms and Bandcamp.

Mari Kattman on self-worth and letting go

“It’s In The Losing You” follows Kattman’s own account of the song’s theme: a refusal to keep seeking validation from others after a lifetime of doing so. The track keeps the electro-industrial sound of her other work, built this time around the idea that self-worth does not depend on anyone else’s approval.

About Mari Kattman

Mari Kattman is a musician, songwriter, producer and vocalist based in Boston, Massachusetts, self-recording, composing, producing and performing live since 2012. Her work combines synth-pop, EBM and industrial influences, and she has built a wide list of collaborations across the electronic music scene, including with Mesh, Rotersand, Neuroticfish, Comaduster and Caustic.

In 2025, Kattman announced her debut full-length for Metropolis Records, “Year Of The Katt”, and shared a video for “Typical Girl” ahead of its release. The album included tracks such as “Anemia” and “Sharp Shooter” alongside “Typical Girl”. Side-Line interviewed Kattman around the album’s release.

Kattman has also toured as part of Assemblage 23’s 2026 European headline run, and contributed vocals to Lords Of Acid’s “Ich Will Nur Das”, released ahead of their album “Mundo Bizarro”.

“It’s In The Losing You”, released November 6, 2026 via Metropolis Records, is Kattman’s latest single after “Year Of The Katt” and her Assemblage 23 and Lords Of Acid collaborations, and she is confirmed to perform at the 2027 edition of M’era Luna Festival in Hildesheim, Germany.

items.title: j:dead closes year-long single campaign with ‘XVII’
items.summary: UK industrial-electronic artist j:dead closes a year-long single campaign with "XVII", released November 6, 2026 via Infacted Recordings.
items.fullText:
UK industrial-electronic artist j:dead has released “XVII” on November 6, 2026 via Infacted Recordings, closing a year-long single campaign that began in December 2025 with “Pressure”.

“XVII” is built around distorted guitar riffs and mid-tempo drums, wrapped in warm, expressive vocals over an industrial base. Instead of closing the campaign with another explosive statement, the track turns inward toward a more measured conclusion.

The song moves between childhood and adulthood, viewing the hopes and dreams of a young man through the perspective of an older self who has lived through more and understands the distance between the person he imagined becoming and the person he became. The title refers to the age of seventeen, the final year of the life j:dead describes before his own story began.

“XVII” was written, performed and recorded by j:dead (Jay Taylor), with guitars by Hilger Tintel and Jay Taylor. Motel-Music produced the track and Studio-600 handled mastering; the artwork is by Dokodemo.

“XVII” is available now on Bandcamp and streaming platforms.

The twelfth single in j:dead’s year-long campaign

j:dead launched the campaign in December 2025 with “Pressure”, followed by “Who Knows” as the third single in January 2026 and a video for “Feeling Alone” in March 2026. Later entries included “Keep Walking”, “Draws My Blood”, “Halo”, “Null” and “Cannibal”, each one released on Infacted Recordings through 2026. “XVII” closes the series as its twelfth and final single.

About j:dead

j:dead is the project of UK musician Jay Taylor. The project makes industrial-electronic music built around distorted guitars, programmed rhythms and emotionally direct songwriting. The project’s catalog includes the singles “Haunt” (2019) and “Feeding On Me” (2020), the album “A Complicated Genocide” (2021), the collaboration “Tearing Me Apart” with Teknovore (2021) and the single “I’ll Wait” (2021).

items.title: “Paris te brutalise, t’immortalise” — French Post-Punk Artist Anton Unveils Video for “Serpent Des Villes”
items.summary: Paris te brutalise, t’immortalise Te brutalise, t’immortalise A city can bruise you and still be the place you most want to remember your name. Paris makes that bargain especially seductive.… The post “Paris te brutalise, t’immortalise” — French Post-Punk Arti
items.fullText:
Paris te brutalise, t’immortalise
Te brutalise, t’immortalise

A city can bruise you and still be the place you most want to remember your name. Paris makes that bargain especially seductive. You go there to become someone, then spend half your time figuring out how to dress, speak, and carry yourself so nobody can tell how badly you want to belong. In Anton’s Serpent Des Villes, black rain comes down, and the city lights go out. By then, Paris has already exacted its tribute. It has taught you to keep up appearances even in the dark.

“Paris te brutalise, t’immortalise,” sings Anton Steinbock. Paris brutalizes you, Paris immortalizes you, and the ease with which one verb follows the other makes the promise sound like a threat. Then comes the refrain, “Y’a rien de pire qu’être parfait” (there’s nothing worse than being perfect), repeated until it sounds as much like a private admonition as a public accusation. Out November 6, “Serpent Des Villes” is the first single from Anton’s forthcoming EP, Tôt Ou Tard.

An organ-like synth picks out a bright, clipped melody over a lower electronic throb and the dry crunch of the drum machine. The French new wave inflection is there before Steinbock sings a word. His voice glides over the beat, giving the French vowels room to stretch while wiry post-punk guitars answer at the ends of his lines. About two-thirds of the way through, the arrangement takes a breath and a rippling bass synth comes forward, giving the song a loose-hipped shuffle on its way to the final refrain. It’s a trick French coldwave has long made its own. The tune is so inviting you catch yourself singing along before you’ve reckoned with the words.

The video finds Steinbock alone in a park, where two crows pick over the lawn and branches fill the frame. He paces, turns with his arms flung out, and brings a hand to his face. From a bench beneath the trees, he sings with the same agitation that sends him back onto the path. By the end, the camera looks up at him against a grey sky and his face is nearly lost in silhouette. He has room to move here, though the urgency of his gestures suggests that getting away from the city and getting it out of your head are two very different things.

Watch the video for Serpent Des Villes below.

Steinbock launched Anton as a solo darkwave project in Paris in 2024, drawing on bands like Joy Division and Lebanon Hanover while singing in French, German, and English. His debut EP Volcan came out that May on Detriti Records, and Anton’s initial live quartet shared bills with TRAITRS, Nürnberg, and Sad Madona. Icy Cold Records issued Glacier / Volcan in March 2025, featuring the standout “L’Autre Destination”. Artist Sylvester Engbrox provided the album artwork and also worked on the videos for the double single Never Freed Myself. Anton played its first international dates in Italy at the end of 2025. The project now performs as a duo, with Steinbock on bass and vocals and artist Gabriela Guyez on synths and vocals.
